Deep learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) are frequently used for time series forecasting due to their flexibility in handling varying time series data. TCNs employ a mechanism called causal convolution that overlooks future data points and uses a trimming function to disregard past information considered irrelevant. However, this approach tends to treat all input data as equally important, relying on the network to automatically eliminate unnecessary past information. In practice, this can result in inefficient network architectures that require a substantial number of parameters to produce optimal results. To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel trimming in time (Trimming In Time, or PIT) module that allows for selective use of past data points, thereby enabling more compact and efficient network architectures. The proposed PIT module is straightforward to integrate into existing TCNs through a layer-wise trimming approach, is computationally lightweight, and is robust in scenarios with limited data. extensive empirical evaluations across 15 diverse time series forecasting tasks and datasets showcase the effectiveness of PIT in achieving a suitable balance between performance and parameter efficiency. The proposed framework is an attractive alternative to other trimming methods, such as sliding window and Fourier Transform-based approaches, due to its superior efficiency in terms of model size. The source code of the proposed trimming method is also made available with clear instructions for replication. Furthermore, this study provides a comprehensive examination of the Pit's module architectural components and their influence on forecasting performance. A critical aspect highlighted by this research is the need for further research into the selective use of past data points for various forecasting tasks. The proposed Trimming In Time (PIT) module has the potential to enhance the efficiency of TCN-based time series forecasting models without compromising performance. In contrast to previous approaches that overlook future data points, the proposed PIT module is unique in its ability to discard unnecessary past information. Although this study only evaluated the proposed module on TCN-based models, it is possible that similar trimming approaches could also be beneficial for other models that employ sliding window convolution, such as Graph Convolutional Networks and Dilated Convolutional Networks. Therefore, researchers are encouraged to explore similar trimming methods in conjunction with these models, as well as Future Vision Networks that look ahead in time, in order to optimize their architecture. The proposed Trimming In Time (PIT) module is an innovative solution that addresses the issue of unnecessary past information in time series forecasting. We introduce Neural Description Fields (NDFs), a novel deep learning framework that treats object detection and pose estimation as a unified problem within the context of incomplete or ambiguous object descriptions. This framework leverages SE(3) symmetry to create a symmetric object representation, ensuring that the same object represented in different poses or orientations is treated as the same entity. During training, NDFs use a symmetric loss function that penalizes inaccuracies in object poses, enabling the model to capture a range of pose variations without explicit pose labels. At inference time, this symmetry allows the model to generate a range of possible object configurations, or "poses," given a description, effectively solving the object pose problem. We apply NDFs to the problem of grasping in clutter, demonstrating that they outperform existing methods while requiring no pose labels, thus providing a more versatile and practical solution for real-world robotics applications. This paper addresses this problem by combining clustering and a pose estimation method using neural networks. Finally, P3P algorithms are used on the points with the highest confidence within each cluster to estimate the pose, and the poses are merged by analyzing the points' confidence and 3D coordinates. This research introduces a novel acoustic lens material called ZrTiO4, also known as zirconium titanate, which can significantly expand the detection range of photoacoustic imaging systems. The characteristics of this material were investigated using numerical models and experimental samples. Our simulations and test results indicate that ZrTiO4 offers high sensitivity and a large extension factor, outperforming current widely used materials like PMMA. Our data shows that ZrTiO4 maintains its high performance even when thin layers are used, which is essential for avoiding excessive tissue penetration. To demonstrate its practical effectiveness, ZrTiO4 was integrated into a photoacoustic breast imaging system and shown to produce clear images of tumors. The findings of this research could lead to the development of more efficient and cost-effective large-area detectors for photoacoustic imaging. Additionally, we explored incorporating multiple layers of ZrTiO4, which showed promising results, which could further improve the detection capabilities of such systems. However, more research is needed to fully understand the effects of using these stacked layers. These advancements hold promise for enhancing the performance of photoacoustic imaging systems, particularly in the detection of small tumors. Our results also suggest that ZrTiO4 could be an ideal material for increasing the sensitivity of ultrasonic transducers used in other medical imaging techniques, such as elastography and thermography, which rely on the conversion of temperature changes into ultrasonic waves. Our research provides a theoretical basis for the optimization of ZrTiO4-based detectors and could pave the way for the development of more efficient temperature-sensing ultrasound transducers. These improvements in detection technology could lead to better tumor localization and more accurate readings of tissue elasticity and temperature, ultimately enhancing the effectiveness of cancer treatment. In complex systems, where relationships between entities are interdependent and multi-faceted, identifying prominent features requires a comprehensive approach that accounts for the varied aspects of the underlying network. Consequently, many real-world networks necessitate a reevaluation of traditional concepts, such as eigenvector centrality, to accommodate their unique characteristics. This study builds upon existing work, refining the eigenvector centrality formula to accommodate networks with significant node interdependencies, where the importance of a node is directly proportional to the sum of the importance of connected nodes, weighted by the strength of those connections. This modified formula, applicable to multi-layer networks, incorporates a non-linear aspect, with implications for network analysis and the detection of prominent features. A key contribution of this research is the introduction of a new centrality measure, eigenvector prominence, which provides a more accurate and comprehensive approach to identifying crucial components and patterns within complex, multifaceted networks. This proposed measure is illustrated through its application to an example network and a comparison made with existing centrality measures, such as eigenvector centrality and R-Louder. A key aspect of this research is the incorporation of node significance, with a focus on its potential to enhance the detection of prominent features in complex, multifaceted networks. This is particularly relevant in the analysis of social networks, adaptive networks, and networks with hidden structure, where a node's intrinsic properties and interconnections with surrounding nodes influence its central position within the network. This research focuses on unstructured raw image noise removal. Unlike demosaiced and deblurred images, raw images contain unorganized photons without a predefined grid structure, providing all possible frequency information and thereby enhancing flexibility in processing. Furthermore, raw images are often affected by both Gaussian and photon noise as well as partial blurring. Existing approaches to raw image processing have employed a collaborative framework that combines deblurring, demosaicing, and denoising tasks. In line with this strategy, our work introduces a novel unstructured raw image noise removal model based on a demosaicing-deblurring-denoising collaborative framework. The model utilizes a demosaicing-deblurring process equivalent to a minimal solution to a constrained optimization problem and leverages a non-local means filter for denoising. However, due to the complexity of optimizing multiple tasks simultaneously, our proposed framework involves an alternating algorithm to solve the problem, enabling efficient computation using conventional optimization methods. Experimental results show that our model outperforms state-of-the-art raw image demosaicing and deblurring approaches, demonstrating the effectiveness of a collaborative framework in enhancing processing flexibility and overall performance. Raw image data is sourced from a Sony A7R II camera, with both synthetic and real-world blurring scenarios tested. Code is publicly available for replication. Our model's performance surpasses existing methods for raw images, suggesting the potential for further research in unstructured raw image processing. In particular, our work may facilitate exploration of more adaptable models in this domain. Additionally, future researchers are encouraged to explore additional features and noise models in this field. Experimental evaluations against a publicly available benchmark indicate that our model excels in reconstructing natural images, including those with blurred and distorted versions of Landmark images, and examples of Flickr photos. In this paper, we examine the optimal margin for a linear program that generates complete and minimal sets of Dirac's variational principles, across Minkowski spacetimes defined by a symmetric matrix $R$ with dimensions $n\times n$. The purpose of this analysis is to extend the established results of Bergman and Teiseierovin for the standard Minkowski spacetime to a broader class of $R$-Minkowski spacetimes. To achieve this, we first establish a comprehensive set of conditions for complete and minimal sets of Dirac's variational principles within the context of Minkowski spacetimes defined by a symmetric matrix $R$. We then demonstrate that any complete and minimal set of solutions can be parameterized by a specific set of linear programs, and conversely, that any linear program with a specific structure yields a complete and minimal set of solutions. Building upon this connection, we are able to prove the optimal margin theorem for linear programs within the context of Minkowski spacetimes defined by a symmetric matrix $R$. The proof strategy relies on a combination of techniques from matrix theory, including results on the stability of elliptic conic sections and the characteristic polynomial of the Gramian matrix. Additionally, we provide a geometric interpretation of the optimal margin by demonstrating that the optimal margin is equal to the radius of the largest ellipsoid contained within a specified convex set defined by a matrix $R$ and vector $b$. Finally, we conclude by outlining potential directions for further research in this area. Additionally, we provide a supplemental online appendix that complements the results presented in this paper. The appendix is available under the journal's open-access policy. The results presented in this paper will be a key component of an upcoming thesis dissertation. We discovered that full-state observation assumes a consistent and uncorrupted state space is maintained during operation, but in reality, it is frequently compromised due to sensor malfunctions, system collisions and falls, and other common issues in robotics. We distinguish between two primary sources of state space corruption: severe (or high-magnitude) and mild (or low-magnitude) corruption. Our research specifically targets severe data degradation, which drastically alters the distribution of available data and significantly hinders the learning efficiency of reinforcement learning methods using policy gradients via corrupt state observations. To mitigate this issue, we proposed an initial clean experience phase, where the agent explores the environment under no noise, and its experience is used to initialize its policy network. Our results demonstrate that this approach yields substantial improvements in learning speed and performance, amounting to up to $10\times$ and $5\times$ respectively, in multiple challenging robotic tasks against severe data degradation. Notably, our solution achieves near-optimal performance without relying on additional clean data, tailored reward functions, or expert interventions. Our research also reveals the value of exploring the environment under no noise, resulting in clean state-action pairs that reduce the policy gradient estimation bias. Building on this insight, we introduce an adaptive clean experience phase size, calculated as the product of the amount of data required to achieve a desired performance and a data efficiency factor, indicating the agent should learn from data that reduces its estimated loss by a certain factor. Our results with this adaptive approach, although not as effective as our initial clean experience phase solution, show they are always superior to not using an adaptive clean experience phase. Our research is significant because it addresses a pervasive issue in robotics that until now has not been the focus of enhanced data efficiency in reinforcement learning. Our solutions can be applied to various challenging robotic tasks, including those with complex physics, multiple objects, and varied environments, and our results provide insights into optimizing reinforcement learning with policy gradients. Our code is available at https://github.com/author name/resilient-pg. Our research offers several real-world applications, including enhancing the robustness of learning in robotics by mitigating the impact of sensor noise, facilitating the transfer of learned skills to environments with different levels of data corruption, and accelerating the training of multiple related tasks with shared data corruption issues. Our research raises several new challenges, including developing efficient methods for detecting severe data degradation during reinforcement learning, introducing alternative clean experience phase solutions, and exploring effective approaches for adaptive hyperparameter tuning in reinforcement learning. As the dark exciton wavefunction develops over time, its probability distribution shows an intriguing correlation with the absolute value of the reduced mass of the exciton, providing a fundamental mass-sensitive indicator. This unique property enables massive Rabi oscillations, and the associated amplitude can be significantly enhanced by selecting wavepackets with appropriate masses, potentially surpassing existing records for dark excitons. A theoretical model, supported by numerical simulations, demonstrates the feasibility of achieving massive Rabi oscillations and offers practical guidelines for experimental implementation. Given the rising complexity of these interactive bots, guided by strategic language generation algorithms, the need for a reliable and standardized evaluation method has never been more pressing. To address this need, we present a pioneering automated assessment framework that streamlines the evaluation process for conversational bots in various scenarios. This innovative approach leverages a combination of natural language processing techniques, including sentiment analysis and dialogue act classification, to comprehensively assess the performance of these systems. We showcase the efficacy of this framework through a case study involving the evaluation of multiple English-language conversational bots. Our methodology offers a versatile evaluation tool that can be adapted to accommodate various dialogue scenarios and languages. The development of this evaluation framework has been made open-source, enabling the community to build upon this work. Furthermore, we introduce a new, publicly accessible evaluation platform that enables researchers and developers to automate the evaluation process for their own conversational bots. This platform is designed to facilitate collaboration and data sharing, paving the way for large-scale, unified evaluations across the field of conversational systems. This collaborative approach is anticipated to propel the advancement of more effective and engaging conversational bots. The existence of an undiscovered planet beyond Neptune's orbit has long been hypothesized based on the orbital patterns of extreme trans-Neptunian objects. By applying the rules of proportionality to the gravitational effect on nearby celestial bodies, researchers have identified potential indicators of such a planet's presence. However, its size and orbital distance remain uncertain variables that significantly impact the outcome. A numerical model is used to assess the impact of various planetary configurations on the gravitational pull on the known planets and their moons, as well as on the detection of the planet's influence, taking into account the current precision of measurements. A hidden planet with a mass similar to that of Uranus or Neptune, located at an average distance of about 200 to 500 astronomical units from the Sun, would likely cause an irregularity in the known planets' orbital paths that is beyond current measurement precision limits. A planet of the same mass but at a much greater orbital distance would only slightly distort its nearby celestial bodies' paths, making it detectable only when the planet and the celestial body are at their closest approach. For example, a hidden planet with an orbital path that brings it within about 200 astronomical units of the Earth by the year 2100 can be confirmed by observing the slight irregularities in the Earth's orbital path around that time. Similarly, a hidden planet can be confirmed by comparing its gravitational effect on the interior and the exterior of the Earth's orbit. The model also highlights that a hidden planet can be confirmed by comparing its gravitational effect on the interior and the exterior of the Earth's orbit. The model further reveals that a hidden planet with an orbital path that brings it within about 50 astronomical units of the Saturnian system by the year 2050 can be confirmed by observing the slight irregularities in the Saturnian system's orbital path around that time. The model's results also indicate that a hidden planet with a mass similar to that of the Earth but at an average distance of about 100 astronomical units from the Sun to the Earth cannot be confirmed by present-day tracking of the known planets due to the extremely small effect of its gravitational pull on their orbital paths, although it would cause a significant distortion in the orbits of the terrestrial planets and their moons. The model's findings provide a basis for the optimal design of follow-up astrometric observations of a hidden planet, as well as for the new data collection that will result from an increased precision in the measurement of the gravitational effect on nearby celestial bodies. To this end, we propose an unsupervised prototype-finding method that reduces prototype selection to a clustering task, leveraging both inter-class and intra-class information to guide our approach. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the widespread issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Many real-world platforms feature multiple sparse domains, where recommendations are sought for various target domains leveraging auxiliary information from multiple secondary domains. To address this complex multi-sparse-domain problem, we introduce a novel approach called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation based on Improved Thorough Aspect Preference Learning. Our method involves a comprehensive multi-aspect preference learning model that captures diverse user preferences in each secondary domain, and a data-interpolation technique that generates rich target domain data by probability-based interpolation. We preform extensive experiments on two real-world datasets, showcasing our approach's superiority over existing cross-domain and multi-domain methods. Notably, our results indicate that our method surpasses both domain-specific models and yields significant improvements in accuracy, with an average gain of 132% in recommendation diversity. Our implementation is efficient, achieving a 10-fold improvement in training time compared to previous multi-task models. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zheng-hu/IMSDL. Further, we investigate the efficacy of different model sizes and confirm that our approach's performance scales well with model size. Our findings validate the practical value of our method in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we explore the impact of target domain data size and find that our approach excels in large-data settings. Our research also delves into the effect of the number of auxiliary domains and reveals that our method effectively leverages up to five auxiliary domains. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art cross-domain and multi-domain methods in terms of precision, recall, diversity, and diversity preservation. Our work also involves a thorough analysis of latent user preference and provides theoretical justifications for our approach's design. Additionally, we introduce an open-source dataset collection framework that automates data cleaning, splitting, and sampling for cross-domain and multi-domain recommendation datasets. Our framework's data sampling module is inspired by the data interpolation technique presented in this study. This data sampling approach is employed in our experiments to validate the efficacy of our method. Our research is also accompanied by an in-depth discussion on the practical applications, challenges, and future research directions in the field of cross-domain and multi-domain recommendation. We present an open-source Julia package called Hypatia for solving second-order cone programs with general positive semi-definite matrices. Despite the vast presence of conic optimization tools, our method stands out as it converts any given organcic conic formulation into a series of simpler representations that can be solved by existing Julia solvers. Specifically, we demonstrate that any positive semi-definite matrix can be decomposed into a specific combination of standard second-order cones along with a diagonal matrix. This fundamental concept serves as the basis for our resolution function. Furthermore, we explore various applications of Hypatia by comparing its performance to that of leading conic optimization solvers and even integrating it with JuMP for solving large-scale sparse problems. Our research also delves into identifying essential and sufficient conditions for positive semi-definite matrices, in addition to examining ways to reformulate other important conic formulations, including semidefinite programs and matrix factorizations. Ultimately, our work aims to provide an efficient yet versatile framework for solving a broad range of conic optimization problems. The rising demand for involving imaging data in medical research and improving patient outcomes relies heavily on creating and annotating high-quality cerebral MRI databases. Unfortunately, labeling MRI quality is a complex task for non-experts due to the subtle nature of certain defects, and relying on radiologists for quality assessment is not feasible because of the time-consuming and costly process involved. This paper explores the possibility of training models to automate the quality assessment process of cerebral MRI scans. This task requires multi-dimensional generalization because the model must simultaneously consider multiple imaging characteristics and a specific grading metric. Our findings indicate that natural language processing tools can effectively capture the dimensional aspects by combining semantic and visual characteristics of the scans, and that using multiple grading criteria actually simplifies the learning process. Our best model achieves a 0.38 correlation with human ratings, demonstrating that automatic assessment performs as well as human experts. This model exhibits comparable performance when tested with unseen data, demonstrating strong generalizability. This research provides the first large-scale data set (3,000 labeled images) and a novel automatic quality assessment reference framework that can be applied to other medical imaging applications. The growing number of privately owned electric vehicles is significantly impacting urban distribution networks, necessitating a new perspective that views them as both loads and reserve resources. However, the current research lack a comprehensive mathematical model that incorporates the complex interplay between these vehicles and the underlying distribution network. This paper introduces a novel multi-agent optimization framework to examine the impact of privately owned electric vehicles on the resilience of urban distribution networks. We developed a detailed multi-agent optimization model that accounts for the decision-making processes of individual drivers, as well as the underlying physics that govern the behavior of the electric vehicles. By utilizing a decomposition-and-coordination approach, we integrated the individual agent models into a cohesive framework that can efficiently solve real-world problems. Our proposed framework is then applied to a numerical case study to illustrate its effectiveness and the complex effects of privately owned electric vehicles on the resilience of urban distribution networks. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the driving patterns and reserve capabilities of these vehicles as both loads and resources, which significantly affects the resilience of the distribution network. This research provides a new perspective on the complex interplay between privately owned electric vehicles, driving patterns, and distribution network resilience, which can be further explored and developed into an efficient solution method. Lattice QCD calculations allow for predictions of physical properties of hadrons, and in this study, we examine potential exotic hadrons consisting of three quarks (baryons) and one quark and one antiquark (mesons) to determine their stability.  By analyzing properties of mesons with one quark and one antiquark, we explore the role of quark flavor and whether meson masses are affected by quark color.  Regarding baryons with three quarks, we investigate the importance of specific quark combinations and the impact of quark color on their masses.  By combining these findings, we create a comprehensive table forecasting the properties of hundreds of extra baryons and mesons awaiting discovery.  Quark flavor is found to govern meson masses, and color does not significantly contribute until quark masses become very small, as in the case of up-quark masses.  In baryons, the most stable compositions are those with one quark flavor and two quarks that attract each other, and a schism appears in baryon masses, with those involving light up-quarks and down-quarks being driven by color and those involving heavy quarks being governed by quark flavor.  By considering both flavor and color, the mass spectra of baryons can be intricately understood, and a Schrödinger-like equation is introduced to illustrate this relationship.  The predictions made in this study can be useful for experimental searches and potential discoveries of extra baryons and mesons. The Lattice Strong Interaction Data Group is encouraged to incorporate these results into their data compilations. Finally, the theoretical foundations of this study are based on the principles of lattice QCD, and the results are consistent with the rules of the Lattice Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) game. These are lecture notes for a 6-hour mini-course on stochastic partial differential equations presented at the University of Oxford in April-May 2021. 

The aim of these lecture notes is to provide an in-depth exploration of the fundamental concepts and techniques in SPDEs. 

The chosen approach is to focus on the abstract approach, specifically leveraging the tools and methods developed in the context of Banach and Hilbert spaces. 

The underlying theory of stochastic analysis, including Ito integrals, stochastic integrals, and stochastic differential equations, is thoroughly examined within the framework of Banach and Hilbert spaces. 

The chapter on stochastic analysis is followed by an examination of different types of SPDEs, including those with a trace operator, hemi-continuuous operators, monotone operators, and operators with a compact variation. 

The lecture concludes with the application of the abstract approach to specific types of SPDEs.

This research paper proposes a new method for efficient data collection in sensor networks by dividing the network into hierarchical areas and establishing reliable paths. The proposed system consists of two layers: the first layer uses a simple algorithm to create circular sectors, while the second layer builds upon this by dividing these sectors into smaller areas using the boundaries of the inner triangles of the circumcircle. A reliable path is established in the second layer by calculating the shortest path length from each inner triangle to the center of the circle. This method is then used to estimate the distance of nodes in the second layer to the center of the circle, allowing for the exclusion of nodes with longer paths. We introduce a novel entity suggestion approach based on an innovative embedding technique for entities connected through layers of information within Wikipedia. Our proposed method, Wikipedia Knowledge Graph Embedding, leverages a unique hierarchical structure found across Wikipedia pages to create an entity suggestion framework. We utilize a particular set of Wikipedia pages, namely biographical articles, to build the Knowledge Graph of Wikipedia. By mapping entities within this graph to a numerical coordinate space, our approach enables the generation of an embedding for each entity based on its presence in the graph. We employ this embedding to develop a straightforward entity suggestion framework, where the suggestion is made by identifying entities geographically close to a given entity to a certain distance. The Ideal Kidney Match problem has long been a subject of interest for mathematicians and computer scientists in its own right, and also as a simplification of complex problems in resource allocation and combinatorial optimization. We present a new formula for calculating the minimum number of pairs that must be ruled out for a set of kidneys to be usable in a matching program, and provide a corresponding algorithm that efficiently identifies an ideal set of kidneys that meet specific criteria under certain conditions. Furthermore, we introduce a new concept called ideal acceptance, and demonstrate that determining ideal acceptance for a given set of kidneys is equivalent to solving a specific variant of the Ideal Kidney Match problem. We also discuss potential applications and extensions of these ideals, and examine how they relate to existing solutions and challenges in computer science. Additionally, we provide a new formulation for solving the Ideal Kidney Match problem, and show that this formulation is equivalent to solving a pair of matching problems in a specific graph structure. We also investigate how the density of the input set affects the performance of algorithms solving the Ideal Kidney Match problem, and demonstrate that there are certain conditions under which a proposed algorithm meets the requirements for ideal acceptance. Finally, we investigate how the Ideal Kidney Match problem relates to other problems in computer science and mathematics, and discuss potential extensions and generalizations of its solutions.

Our study examines the top quark polarization at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) in t-channel single top quark production. To achieve this, we determine the polarization sensitivity in various decay modes of the top quark, specifically focusing on its relation to angular distributions and polarization observables. In t-channel single top quark production, the W boson's transverse momentum and the forward-scattered proton's direction provide crucial information on the top quark's polarization. However, these also increase the background's rejection threshold. As a result, the most polarization-sensitive configurations emerge in events where the top quark fragments into a bottom quark and a W boson that subsequently decays into electrons or muons. For these outcomes, we find that with an integrated luminosity of 300 inverse femtobarns (fb^-1), the top quark polarization can be measured with an accuracy of better than 0.05 at 95% confidence level. Unlike other datasets, MultiTalk's turn-based labeling scheme acknowledges the varied structure of conversations, making it an invaluable resource for researchers who aim to create conversation models capable of complex, sustained dialogue. We've introduced the MultiTalk Dialogue Framework, a first of its kind, which incorporates multiple topic-based conversations into a single discussion by introducing a new interaction model and establishing a labeling scheme that prioritizes branching markers. Our evaluation of the MultiTalk Dialogue Framework reveals that incorporating dialogue history and topic transitions through bidirectional and self-supervised attention modules significantly enhances the natural language evaluation results of our conversation models. Our findings demonstrate that this approach leads to more human-like conversations by enabling these models to engage in complex discussions. We introduce a novel method for conducting comprehensive N-body simulations across various altered gravity scenarios, leveraging an all-encompassing potential model that unifies $f(R)$ gravity, Brans-Dicke theory, and conformally coupled theories. By defining a universal metric potential $\psi$ such that $f(\psi) = 8\pi G$, we reformulate these theories' effects on gravity using a link function $A$ that bridges the standard Einstein gravity and its modified counterparts. Our approach allows for the incorporation of a wide range of altered gravity models, from $f(R)$ and Brans-Dicke to $\Lambda$CDM, through appropriate choices of the link function, potential, and a dimensionless constant $\beta$ that links the Brans-Dicke parameter to the Ricci scalar. We develop an efficient algorithm for solving the conformal Einstein field equations numerically, circumventing the need for an iterative method. Our method also facilitates direct integration of the equations using a compact closed form, thus significantly enhancing the computational cost. We verify our method by simulating a single modified gravitational wave propagation scenario, comparing our results to existing studies. Furthermore, we explore the behavior of altered gravity simulations for $f(R)$ and Brans-Dicke models, demonstrating how our method accommodates a wide range of model variations. Our approach offers a versatile tool for swiftly exploring the effects of diverse modified gravity models, from Brans-Dicke to $\Lambda$CDM, through a comprehensive N-body simulation framework. This study paves the way for a deeper exploration of how our method affects galaxy formation simulation results, including maps of gas and stellar distributions, star formation rates, and agn activity. Our method is also adaptable to existing galaxy formation simulation software, such as EAGLE and EAGarvE, for a more in-depth analysis of modified gravity simulations. We make our method's numerical solution publicly available for further research use. Additionally, we outline potential research directions for further investigation. Our method's unique feature is its direct integration of the altered gravity field equations, in contrast to the majority of numerical simulations that employ iterative methods. We investigate the computational advantages of our direct integration approach, discovering a significant improvement in the accuracy of our results, specifically in the modified gravitational wave waveform, particularly in the high-frequency component. We explore various altered gravity models using our method, including $f(R)$ and Brans-Dicke theories, as well as $\Lambda$CDM, for both their potential impact on dark matter and dark energy

This research addresses a key challenge in fire suppression: understanding how turbulent flame dynamics are affected by building vibrations. To tackle this, a new method is developed to create unstable flame waves using internal heat sources that mimic external disturbances such as acoustic fields. The approach involves using a linearized combustion model with a closed-form solution, and it is applied to a one-dimensional model of a jet fire. The resulting method is then expanded to predict how the flame responds to acoustic fields, specifically for predictions of heat flux and flame temperature. To verify the approach, comparisons are made with existing models, including an active flame model and a model of unstable flame waves. The developed method is then used to investigate the effects of acoustic fields on a turbulent jet fire, including how different frequencies and amplitudes influence heat transfer and flame temperature. The study reveals how heat flux and temperature respond to acoustic excitation, particularly showing how increased frequency leads to larger variations in heat transfer and temperature to a point, before diminishing as frequency continues to increase. The method also highlights how amplitude affects the flame's response, with larger amplitudes leading to greater variations in heat transfer and temperature at specific frequencies. The study also explores how different frequency and amplitude combinations affect heat transfer and temperature, including the emergence of secondary peaks in heat transfer when the Grashof number is 10 to the power of 7, but not at a lower Grashof number of 10 to the power of 6. The method demonstrates its applicability to predicting heat transfer and temperature in response to acoustic fields, and it offers a potential solution to the challenge of fire suppression in structures experiencing vibrations due to flow-induced acoustic fields. The method is suitable for predicting heat transfer and temperature in jet fires with a high Grashof number of 10 to the power of 8, but further research is needed to generalize its findings to fires with lower Grashof numbers, particularly number of 10 to the power of 6. The study also recommends exploring alternative methods for predicting heat transfer and temperature in fires with lower Grashof numbers, including models of unstable flame waves and active flame models. The method is a significant contribution to the field of fire safety, and it has significant implications for the design of safe structures in flows with high Grashof numbers. The study provides a foundation for further research into the effects of acoustic fields on turbulent flames, and it offers a suite of recommendations for future research projects in fire safety. The method is a critical component of safe structure design, and it must be integrated into fire safety codes

The unexplored nature of ultra-high energy photons streaming from the sun fosters speculation about their origins, potentially linking them to cosmic rays' sources or the solar magnetic field's structure. To gain insight, we simulate the interaction of these photons with solar magnetic fields using a linear response approximation, considering energies ranging from 10 to 500 MeV. By examining field strengths from $10^4$ to $10^9$ Gauss, we investigate how the absorption coefficient varies with energy, magnetic field intensity, and the angle between the photon direction and the magnetic field. Our simulations reveal that for energies above 100 MeV, the absorption coefficient exhibits only slight changes with energy, concentration instead on the field's intensity and orientation. Moreover, our simulations demonstrate that the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index exhibit distinct relationships with the photon energy, magnetic field intensity, and the angle between the photon direction and the magnetic field. Furthermore, we find that the ratio of the real part to the imaginary part of the refractive index is directly proportional to the square of the photon energy, the square of the magnetic field strength, and the cosine of the angle between the photon direction and the magnetic field. By exploring different solar magnetic field configurations, we provide theoretical foundations for experimental verification of these simulations through the observation of solar gamma-ray spectra. For example, the simulation of an isotropic gamma-ray flux with an energy spectrum and a solar magnetic field strength of approximately $10^8$ Gauss can be tested by searching for specific spectral signatures in data from satellite-based gamma-ray detectors. Such testing has the potential to contribute to our understanding of high-energy physics and the solar magnetic field. Furthermore, the principles derived from these simulations can be applied to the investigation of gamma-ray interactions within magnetic fields in various astrophysical contexts. Additionally, we propose that the name "Mróz" be assigned to this new phenomenon. Furthermore, we provide theoretical evidence that the solar magnetic field can induce the Mie scattering of ultra-high energy photons, resulting in the stream described as Mie stream or Mróz stream. According to Einstein's general theory of relativity, the curvature of spacetime is affected by the presence of mass and energy. This predicts specific relationships between the geometric and physical properties of gravitational fields, particularly in contexts where gravity is so intense that other theories are not applicable, such as in black holes and neutron stars. A crucial aspect of these predictions involves the 'bending of light', which can be verified by observing the way light is deflected as it passes near these massive objects. The amount of deflection is directly related to the mass of the object and its distance from the light. The ratio of this deflection to the angle of separation forms a constant, often referred to as $\gamma$. The value of this constant is 1.758 when considering the deflection of light by a point mass and its relationship to the mass and distance from the point mass. However, the way light behaves when it is emitted from a source that is emitting both radio waves and light provides additional information about $\gamma$. The ratio of the angle of separation in the two forms of electromagnetic radiation is determined by the emission's properties rather than the mass of the gravitational field it is passing through. The challenge lies in using this approach to make precise measurements of $\gamma$ without being contaminated by noise in the data, especially since the signal is typically weak and is being observed over long periods. By applying advanced statistical techniques to existing data from the binary pulsar PSR B1913+16, a value of $\gamma$ is derived that is independent of general relativity and confirms its accuracy. The precision of this measurement is currently limited by the available data, but it is anticipated that future observations from the Galactic Center with radio waves and light emitted from Sgr B2 will enable more precise measurements with a value of $\gamma$ that could be up to ten times more accurate. The goal of incremental learning is to train a model on continuously arriving data from multiple categories while preventing memory-based contamination and category drift. In real-world scenarios, certain categories may dominate others due to differing densities, resulting in an imbalance problem that significantly complicates the incremental learning task. As a result, the usual all-or-nothing memory update strategy is rendered ineffective, leading to poor performance on sparse categories. Moreover, existing incremental learning algorithms fail to address the specific challenges of incrcal learning with imbalanced data. Our research fills this critical knowledge gap by introducing a new approach that incorporates both category-based and sample-based memory update strategies as well as a novel algorithm to tackle the challenges of imbalanced incral learning. We compare our proposed method to multiple baseline methods, including our own implementation of previous state-of-the-art incral learning algorithms, confirming the superior performance of our approach, particularly on datasets with significant density disparities. Our experiments also demonstrate the benefits of our technique when compared to simply applying techniques to process imbalanced data in each individual batch. Using robotic tools to study human locomotion, this research reveals a surprising finding that contrary to common assumptions, adding power to bipedal movement does not necessarily enhance speed or stability. In fact, it can even impede progress. This discovery is the foundation for developing more effective and resilient walking patterns, and we explore ways to optimize movement with the aid of external power. By examining various control methods and experimenting with different levels of power, we identify conditions that produce desired outcomes, such as increasing walking speed without compromising stability. Our research demonstrates that, with proper assistance, speed can be improved significantly, even exceeding anticipated limits, and highlights the potential for treating movement disorders like stroke-induced gait difficulties with powered leg prosthetics. The most efficient control methods, direct force control and zero-moment velocity, were found to be more resistant to external disturbances and power fluctuations, while our experiments with 25% more powerful actuators showed that higher power inputs can yield faster walking speeds, although this may compromise stability and needs further study. The findings of this research can serve as a basis for exploring other complex human movements like running, climbing stairs, and walking on uneven terrain. Recent research emphasizing through-silicon wave propagation has led to the development of novel, higher-performance computing techniques, yet scaling these approaches to large, practical applications remains a significant challenge.  We address this issue by introducing a new, pioneering method, extending existing concepts in light-speed computing and virtual prototyping, yet taking a completely different approach.  Our proposed system, based on slowly traversing light waves across millions of feet of silicon, leverages the material's inherent properties to perform calculations by harnessing the inherent time delays inherent to the dielectric properties of silicon.  We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach by applying it to the matrix multiplication algorithm, achieving accurate results and mapping the application efficiently across a large chip.  Our experiments, conducted on a state-of-the-art 80-core research chip, show that despite significant wave propagation losses, our proposed method yields significant performance gains, with results comparable to custom-designed, high-speed matrix multiplication code but with much simpler hardware.  We also explore ways to further optimize our technique by scaling our application to smaller, smaller sizes, leveraging the insights gained to guide the design of larger, practical applications for future research chips.  Our work showcases the potential of wave-based computing to enhance the efficiency of traditional CPU programming, with potential applications in domain-specific hardware and potentially even cross-domain research.  We also introduce a new open-source research framework that integrates our proposed method with existing research tools, making it easier to experiment with wave-based computing and provide the preliminary wave-profilng data for our research chip, a valuable resource for the broader research community.  We believe that our work represents an important step in exploring the boundaries of what can be achieved with wave-based computing and hope that our findings will motivate other researchers to explore this exciting area of research. To facilitate such measurements, it is essential to understand the theoretical $Z$ decay width, particularly its gamma component, which arises from loop interactions and contributes significantly to the total width. Although this gamma component is generally well understood within the standard model, its interpretation changes when considering extra dimensions or other extensions to the standard model, particularly when such additions affect the weak mixing angle. New research by the KATRIN collaboration provides evidence that electron anti-neutrino masses are restricted below a certain threshold. In this study, we analyze how this discovery affects minimum neutrino mass requirements, focusing on models incorporating magnetic moment interactions. Similar restrictions on neutrino flavors are explored in the context of existing limits set by other experiments and theoretical constraints, particularly those imposed by neutrino oscillation phenomena and the cosmic neutrino background. Additionally, we investigate the implications of these findings for neutrino mass pattern possibilities and the associated magnetic moment or energy range. Existing limits on neutrino masses due to oscillation constraints are found to be more restrictive than those imposed by KATRIN in the low mass range. Nevertheless, the research reveals that sizable regions of neutrino mass spectrum patterns, including the inverted hierarchy type, remain compatible with the KATRIN findings and known experimental limits. In the case of the normal hierarchy, the discovery significantly tightens the minimum mass constraint, particularly for muon neutrinos, exceeding existing oscillation limit in the low mass range. The research also indicates that the restriction imposed by KATRIN on electron anti-neutrino masses may lead to a downward revision of the minimum mass in the range between 0.4 and 1.0 MeV. The available theoretical models, which comprise magnetic moment interactions and R-parity violating supersymmetry, remain within the existing oscillation limit in the low mass range. The research predicts that in the near-future, the KATRIN research will likely further reduce existing minimum mass restrictions by half in the low mass range due to anti-neutrino production via muon decay, resulting in an available neutrino spectrum with a high density above the inherent muon rest mass and extending down to an electron anti-neutrino mass of approximately 0.4 MeV. The proposed Higgs factory projects are expected to surpass these restrictions in the low mass range. The research also indicates that in the high mass range, the existing minimum mass restrictions are likely to be set by the Big Bang Nucleosynthesis, followed by a significant gap in the neutrino mass spectrum. and diverse. To formalize this concept, we introduce a novel measure, extremal
conditional entropy, which can be minimized through an efficient algorithm. Notably,
our results reveal that the optimal solutions for both maximum and minimum conditional
entropy, as well as extremal conditional entropy, can be achieved by clustering the
data, a method previously proven for maximum conditional entropy. Additionally, our
research provides a data-independent solution for minimum conditional entropy, which
can be realized by selecting the most representative centroids. These advances provide
insights into the complex interplay between structure and diversity in conditional
models. Furthermore, our proposed algorithm for extremal conditional entropy is a
semi-supervised clustering method, which is efficient in terms of both computational
requirements and memory usage. We demonstrate the efficacy of these methods on a
variety of synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing their ability to strike a
balance between structure and diversity. Our results also highlight the role of
diversity in conditional models, illustrating how it can significantly impact the

Additionally, our investigation of the one-particle spectrum's scattering rate reveals how it is influenced by both intragenerational and intergenerational interactions. This research focuses on creating Molmer-Sorensen gates that can withstand frequency fluctuations for trapped ions using laser pulses that balance multiple vibrational modes. By employing a balanced superposition of motional modes, we've developed a range of trap-to-rail frequency transformations that allow for precise timing control. As a result, we've minimized the required entanglement times, enabling the construction of robust multi-ion Molmer-Sorensen gates despite frequency fluctuations of up to 100 kHz. A broad spectrum of trapped ions can benefit from this method, particularly those with large mass differences, like aluminum ions paired with laser-cooled ground-state calcium ions. An accompanying demonstration shows the effectiveness of frequency-resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates for quantum teleportation and covariance measurements. Notably, this approach also facilitates the efficient creation of balanced motional states, a crucial resource for various quantum applications. Furthermore, we've found that this method can be adaptation for diamond-based quantum computing, paving the way for the development of large-scale, frequency-resilient quantum networks. This research demonstrates the potential for robust multi-ion operations within the linear trap environment, essential for various quantum applications, including quantum simulation and chemistry experiments. Additionally, we've outlined a strategy for transforming the frequency-balanced molion state into a specific quadrature, enabling the measurement of motional-state-dependent fluorescence, a crucial step for overcomplete quantum teleportation. Overall, this research provides a solution for overcoming frequency imprecision in the linear trap, a crucial challenge in ion-trap quantum computing. The spatiotempally averaged structures of paraelectric perovskites are typically considered uniform, yet they exhibit significant variability when examined at a microscopic level.  Using atomic scale simulations, we found that the microscopic structures of paraelectric ABO3 (AE = Ba, Sr; B = Mn, Fe, Ni) systems are dynamically stable in the paraelectric phase and thus provide a foundation for further investigation into their corresponding ferroelectric properties.  At room temperature, we performed a comprehensive characterization of the microscopic structures via the analysis of pair distribution functions, bond angle distributions, and orientational correlation functions.  We discovered that the microscopically rotated B sites exhibit unique ordering patterns, contributing to the understanding of B cation preferences within the lattice.  Notably, we found that replacing Ba with Sr results in a more disordered state of the A sites, which however does not significantly affect the broader distribution of B-O bond angles and orientations.  We also examined the effects of temperature and lattice parameter changes on the microscopic structures, and we found that both changes provoke a more disordered state of the A sites as well as a broader distribution of B-O bond angles and orientations, which provide valuable insights for experimentalists to reconcile their findings with those of theoretical simulations.  Furthermore, we provide detailed technical guidelines for using pair distribution function analysis and bond angle distribution analysis to reconstruct and assess the structural models derived from inelastic neutron scattering data.  These methodologies are equally applicable to the examination of other materials.  Ultimately, we demonstrate that the unique ordering patterns of the B sites are a crucial factor in the decision of whether a particular perovskite will exhibit a ferroelectric or antiferroelectric behavior.  Specifically, we found that B sites that exhibit 90-degree rotation ordering are more likely to result in a ferroelectric outcome, whereas those that exhibit 180-degree rotation ordering are more likely to yield an antiferroelectric outcome.  This theoretical framework can be applied to the prediction of functional materials in other structural classes.  Finally, we propose that inelastic neutron scattering combined with structural modeling offers a powerful and versatile approach to the in-depth examination of materials, and we anticipate that this methodology will be equally effective when applied to other materials. Power spectrum analyses in various fields, including astrophysics and brain function research, often identify significant features by pinpointing peaks within a given frequency range. However, these methods can be vulnerable to errors due to the inherent properties of power spectra, which are typically evaluated on a logarithmic scale. Our research presents a novel approach, based on an alternative representation of power spectra, that utilizes geometric means instead of conventional arithmetic means. This method offers a more precise way to measure peak significance, taking into account the inherent scaling properties of power spectra. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by reevaluating well-known features in the solar and brain dynamics data using this new method. For instance, we rediscover the widely reported 11-year solar cycle frequency in only three days of solar magnetogram data and significantly improve the accuracy of brain frequency detection. Our research also explores relationships between frequency and period, demonstrating that features at specific frequencies often follow geometric progressions, which can be useful for predicting undiscovered peaks. By integrating our approach into an open-source Python package called pyprobes, we make it easier for researchers to reproduce and extend our findings to their own data. Our framework, which includes tools for data preprocessing, feature detection, and visualization as well as statistical analysis, is now available for the broader scientific community to use. Our code is readily available on GitHub at https://github.com/pspryjoma/pyprobes, and the solar data analysis results are on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6451183, while the brain data analysis findings are on FigShare at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.c5131451.v1. Our research paves the way for an alternative method for discovering features in power spectra and ratios, and we invite other researchers to collaborate and contribute to this approach. By exploring the relationships between frequency and ratio, as well as considering the inherent scaling properties of power spectra, we believe our method will lead to a more precise and effective way of analyzing these types of data. A self-aligned dual facial regression framework is then employed to refine the reconstruction by simultaneously processing both the original image and an occlusion-free coarse-scale representation. By leveraging occlusion information within the image, our method delivers a more realistic and detailed facial surface, as well as improved alignment. Experimental results show our proposed approach outperforms competing methods across multiple evaluation metrics, specifically in terms of robust performance in the presence of heavy occlusions. Our code and data have been made publicly available. Furthermore, we introduce an expanded dataset that contains a diverse range of tightly bound occlusion pairs, obtained through a novel sampling process, in order to facilitate further research in this area. This dataset can be accessed through our project webpage. Our research focuses on chiral Lagrangian theories, where the spontaneous breaking of translation invariance results in two distinct sectors with opposite momentum properties. We identify the low-energy effective theories that emerge in each sector and demonstrate how they give rise to propagating objects, including higher-dimensional branes and strings. Furthermore, we explore how these objects interact with each other through the exchange of Goldstone bosons, describing their behavior as a result of a derivative expansion. The properties of the interacting effective theories are determined using the Goldstone theorem and structural arguments, allowing us to derive the coefficients of the low-energy effective actions. These derivations yield the charge density of a monopole, the tension of a string, and the volume of a 3-brane, demonstrating how they relate to the symmetry-breaking parameters, while also establishing the constraint that the charge density must be a fracton when it is isolated. Additionally, we discuss the distinction between types of fractons, including those related to symmetries, central charges, and number densities, and examine the conditions necessary for deconfinement and monopole instability in 1+1 dimensions. Wireless communication systems are subject to high disruption risks due to the presence of other wireless communication systems, resulting in decreased performance and reliability. This issue is particularly pronounced in urban settings, specifically at road intersections where vehicles are present. As a result, there is a pressing need for next-generation wireless communication standards to address these interference-prone environments. This research assesses the adaptive collaborative protocol of Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NCMA) in urban settings, particularly at road intersections, and compares it to conventional NCMA. The proposed adaptive collaborative NCMA protocol utilizes vehicle-to-everything communication to share their received signal-to-noise ratios, enabling the base station to adapt the coding and modulation levels of user equipment. This approach leads to a significant increase in system sum rate and a notable improvement in system reliability when facing varying levels of interference. However, it comes at the cost of increased overhead in uplink transmissions. Notably, this research finds that the negative impact of this overhead is compensates by the improved performance at high SNR levels. A hybrid discrete-corrective method is employed to analyze this system and simulate scenarios with varying antenna configurations, vehicle densities, and interference levels. The results demonstrate that the proposed adaptive collaborative NCMA protocol provides a substantial increase in system sum rate and reliability, achieving up to 50% more than conventional NCMA. Furthermore, this research identifies that vehicle density has the most significant impact on system performance, followed by antenna configuration and then interference levels. This has significant implications for the design of communication protocols and vehicle density management strategies in urban wireless communication systems. Overall, this research confirms that the proposed adaptive collaborative NCMA protocol is highly effective in urban settings, specifically at road intersections, and is suitable for large-scale cellular networks. This research also provides a framework for further investigation into the performance of NCMA in urban settings, specifically at road intersections, which can be applied to other wireless communication standards. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Despite significant progress in the field, a significant challenge remains, mainly because the gloss provided in a dictionary is often an inaccurate representation of how the word is used in a sentence.  In order to improve the accuracy of WSD models, we propose incorporating contextualized word representations and gloss-related data to train a WSD model.  Our proposed framework, ContextGloss, utilizes the Universal Sentence Encoder to generate context-related representations and a word sense inventory's sense representations.  ContextGloss is then trained using a classification-based approach to resolve WSD, with the goal of optimizing the model's performance by utilizing a large dataset of annotated sentences with the target word's sense labels.  Our experimental results demonstrate that the ContextGloss framework outperforms the current state-of-the-art WSD models on the SemEval-2007 test data.  Furthermore, we observe that the proposed framework's performance is comparable to that of a strong baseline that incorporates pre-trained BERT models, indicating potential applications of the ContextGloss framework to other word sense disambiguation tasks.  Additionally, we explore the possibility of introducing the general context representations and the word's sense representations as additional input to the BERT model, leading to a potential future work section.  In conclusion, the proposed ContextGloss framework offers a feasible solution to addressing the issue of context and gloss-related ambiguities in WSD, and the obtained source codes and models are made readily available for further exploration.  Finally, the paper is concluded with future research directions for the ContextGloss framework. In the context of word sense disambiguation, both the context and the gloss pose significant challenges to achieving accurate disambiguation, and it is essential to incorporate both aspects into a unified model, as neither context nor gloss is sufficient on its own. In a $p$Pb collision at 5.02 TeV or an $A$U collision at 1.04 TeV, the minimum required significance for a fifth quark generation signal is approximately $\sigma \times 2.02$, $\sigma \times 2.05$, or $\sigma \times 2.11$ for $t$-channel production, top quark pair production, and top quark pair production with opposite top quark polarities respectively.

Top quark production in the $t$-channel or in pairs can also serve as signatures in searches for extra dimensions, such as in searches for high-energy jets, missing transverse momentum, or leptonically decaying top quarks.

To this end, we evaluate the present and potential reach of experiments in searching for top quark generation in proton-nucleus collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, taking into consideration both existing and prospective triggers, as well as both current and anticipated sensitivities in searches for beyond-Standard Model phenomena.

For the LHC with its nominal proton-proton beam intensity but operating with proton-nucleus collisions, we find that even with the existing energy range, detection of top quark generation should be feasible by the end of the collider's current run or during its upcoming run with enhanced sensitivity in searches for beyond-Standard Model phenomena. Furthermore, if the LHC's beam intensity is fully utilized but only in proton-proton collisions, the reach in top quark pair production will only reach the minimum mass requirement at the end of the collider's current run. Recent studies on text2sql have focused primarily on natural language prompts derived from existing tables, with minimal work done on parsing free-form texts. We distinguish text2sql from another process, we term as "supportive text2sql", where the input text contains relevant information. We argue that both processes are necessary to interpret a full sentence and combine their outcomes. To handle both cases, we propose an integrated end-to-end model, comprising of two components. The first component, a cross-domain parser, breaks down the input sentence into meaningful components, including identifying the relevant table and constructing the semantic graph regardless of the input. The second component, a low-degree-of-freedom model with pre-trained database information, then uses the graph to determine the column and execute the sql command. We train and evaluate our model on the Spider dataset, with varying prompts and table annotations, to gauge its effectiveness. Our results show that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art baselines in multiple settings. Moreover, we observe a notable boost in performance when the model is trained on a diverse range of prompts and annotations. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangv/s2s. Furthermore, we introduce a new evaluation metric called mean mean average precision, which provides a comprehensive assessment of both precise and loose sql translations. This evaluation metric is now widely adopted in subsequent cross-domain text2sql challenges. In subsequent years, our work inspires numerous cross-domain text2sql challenges and tasks that aim to execute a wide range of sql commands over various databases. Three such challenges and tasks are Spider-2021, SpiderCrosslinguistics-2021, and SpiderVirtual-2021, all built on top of the Spider dataset, with minor modifications to their dataset descriptions. These changes involve adding more looser sql translations to the original Spider dataset, with the aim of executing different sql commands over additional databases. We clarify that although these subsequent challenges and tasks draw inspiration from our work, they are independent research problems that warrant individual investigation. In recent years, research on structured data, specifically graphs, has gained significant momentum. Various high-impact applications that utilize graph data, such as social networks and gene expression networks, have created critical security challenges. Although graph data possesses valuable insight, its sensitive nature demands stringent confidentiality measures. Unfortunately, many existing studies have revealed alarming rates of unauthorized data disclosure due to vulnerabilities in graph databases and processing systems. A growing body of research aims to address these confidentiality breaches by detecting and preventing unwanted information leakage from graph data. This class of research is referred to as differential confidentiality for graph data and is the focus of this comprehensive survey. We have observed an surge in relevant studies in recent years, with distinct goals such as developing secure graph processing frameworks, private machine learning algorithms for graph data, and preventing specific forms of information disclosure. Our work delves into an in-depth examination of existing research on differential confidentiality for graph data, classifying the current state of art into three primary categories: secure graph processing, private machine learning, and leakage-above-baseline attacks. Furthermore, we highlight the limited attention paid to certain aspects of graph data and its applications and also provide insights into potential future research directions for this important field. We hope this work to serve as a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners working on the important topic of differential confidentiality for graph data. Additionally, we have included an appendix with an extended list of included studies as well as a section on upcoming research worth exploration. To accelerate the development of advanced lane-changing systems, research focuses on creating simulated road networks that mimic real-world challenges. However, designing such complex roads requires significant expertise and time. This research creates an automatic system to generate difficult road networks for evaluation purposes. Firstly, a method is devised to create circular sections with varying sizes and positions. Secondly, a set of challenging scenarios is predefined and an algorithm is developed to assemble these scenarios onto the road network. Thirdly, vehicles are generated to test the road network's complexity. The system is tested with different generation parameters to assess its impact on the resulting road networks and the outcomes are compared to versions manually created by experts. The research demonstrates that the automatic system produces road networks just as complex as those created manually. Additionally, the paper explores ways to optimize the algorithm while maintaining the level of complexity. The proposed system is part of a comprehensive lane-changing simulation environment and the source code is made available for download. Melody captioning is a novel music task where a written description is generated to represent a single melody. To test this idea, we propose a new task: creating written descriptions for entire playlists composed of multiple melodies. Achieving this involves not only identifying the central melody but also accurately describing the accompanying melodies in the playlist. To address this challenge with a large number of possible melodies, we present an innovative method called the Central Melody Descriptor Model. Instead of relying on explicit melody recognition, this model leverages a unique descriptor for each melody in the database, effectively using a unique identifier to distinguish them. By doing so, it expands the possibilities for our model to work with any melody, regardless of its popularity. We demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms existing melody-specific models and showcases the potential for our method to handle a wide range of melodies with accuracy. Our proposed approach, DCAN, addresses this issue by using a dual context consolidation network that extracts long-term and short-term context information to refine the classification of events. We pretrain the network on large datasets without segmenting videos, which allows it to recognize patterns within each individual clip. During training, the network identifies potential event start and end points by analyzing both long-term patterns and the specific contents of each video. Notably, we show that DCAN's ability to recognize patterns across all possible video lengths contributes to its high accuracy. Additionally, we explore various context consolidation strategies and demonstrate the benefits of our specific approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/zheng-shirley/DCAN. For complex activities defined by multiple annotations, we introduce a method for sorting activities by the number of contributing segments, and our results indicate that this ordering enhances DCAN's performance. We also examine the possibility of applying DCAN to other object detection tasks. Our results suggest that DCAN excels at detecting spatially distant objects and those with varying scales, which aligns with the characteristics of temporal activity detection. Overall, our results confirm the effectiveness of DCAN for temporal activity detection. Furthermore, we discuss the differences between DCAN and contemporary models, and our findings indicate that the robustness of DCAN is consistent with its context consolidation capabilities. Overall, our results validate the superiority of DCAN for temporal activity detection. The long-lived ELMs with large fluxes, known as large ELMs with low frequencies ('low-freq big ELMs' or LFBs), exhibit distinct characteristics on the JET tokamak, specifically frequent appearances during ELMsytokamak campaigns, tightly correlated electron and ion circulation flow velocities, unusually large detached plasma regions, and localized pedestal mode structures dubbed 'Palm Tree Modes'. Statistical analysis indicates that these modes are linked to the plasma's edge magnetic field properties and circulatory flow phenomena. As a result, a 'Palm Tree Mode' scenario has emerged, suggesting that magnetic field fluctuations cause weakened electron circulation, leading to reduced electron pressure and, in turn, decreased flow velocities and plasma regions as well as mode stability in the ion direction, allowing 'Palm Tree Modes' to persist. Furthermore, when combined with down-turned electron circulation, this scenario produces a pedastal structure analogous to that generated by an ideal MHD model, featuring mode localization in the radial direction. Although 'Palm Tree Modes' may contribute to the formation of low-freq big ELMs, other factors such as edge pedestal stability in the ion direction must also be considered. These findings imply that 'Palm Tree Modes' can prevent ELMs with similar characteristics from striking the lower port, an observation consistent with recent experiments on the MAST tokamak. These discoveries provide a deeper understanding of edge plasma flow and magnetic field interplay and highlight the importance of flow velocities in determining ELM behavior. As a result, future research into the origins of ELMs must take account of both ion and electron circulation flow velocities as well as the relationships between them. We examine the fundamental concepts of Einstein's general relativity, focusing on its seminal 1915 form and the role of the Einstein tensor in describing the geometric structure of gravity. Although the Einstein tensor is a conserved quantity related to the symmetry of the gravitational field, it does not directly appear in the original 1915 papers. Instead, it was introduced by Einstein in 1921 to simplify the laws governing gravitational wave propagation. We also explore alternative formulations of Einstein's theory, including the use of a Lagrangian density to derive the Einstein field equations through variational principles. While these formulations are equivalent to the standard form of general relativity, they provide valuable insights for extending general relativity through modifications of the Lagrangian density, affecting the behavior of gravity at small distances and high energies. Such modifications can be achieved by introducing non-minimal couplings between matter and gravity, violating the weak equivalence principle, or modifying the Einstein-Hilbert action through higher-order terms, new gravitational scalar fields, or non-local interconnections. We discuss the basic properties of these alternative theories, often leading to predictions in concordance with general relativity for most astronomical phenomena but resulting in distinct effects on large cosmic scales, particularly influencing the expansion history of the universe. We also review current and anticipated cosmic probes capable of testing general relativity's extensions, including its implications on the behavior of falling objects, the bending of light, gravitational waves, cosmic expansion, and certain aspects of the early universe. Ultimately, investigating general relativity's extensions offers valuable insights into the fundamental nature of space, time, and matter.
