Classifying musical devices, such as instruments from audio recordings, has long been a challenging music processing problem. Despite significant research in this area, many existing solutions are limited to recognizing common Western instruments, but often fail to identify devices from other cultural contexts, like the sitar. To break down this barrier, a new approach is required. One promising method involves using a hierarchical framework with a high-level category for all musical devices. However, training such a model on a small dataset poses another difficulty. This paper introduces a 101-class hierarchy that encompasses a broad range of musical devices and explores the possibility of using a small dataset of only European instruments to train a model that can accurately identify devices from other cultures. However, due to the large size of the hierarchy and the small size of the dataset, significant overfitting occurs during training. This paper investigates different ways to mitigate this overfitting and evaluates various hyperparameter settings for a method called GroupNorm. The results show that, although the model struggles to recognize some devices from the base dataset during the training process, it is still capable of achieving high accuracy on unseen devices from the same family. The research also indicates that, in some cases, adding more complexity to the model does not necessarily improve its performance and that different types of musical instruments may require different levels of complexity. The proposed approach and the evaluation protocol are also applicable to few-shot learning in other audio classification tasks. The paper further explores combining the hierarchical classification with another classification layer on top of the feature extractor and finds that such a combination can lead to a significant performance boost. The research is ongoing and is being conducted by the authors as part of the Music Processing Seminar 2022 at the University of Oxford. The code and the paper can be found at https://github.com/kuang33/few-shot-musical-device-recognition and will be updated accordingly. The paper will be presented at the 18th International Conference on Music Information Retrieval. The method achieves a mean average precision of 0.2572 on the complete dataset and further explores different types of evaluation metrics. The paper also investigates different ways to expand the base dataset with more European instruments and finds that doing so can lead to a performance boost of up to 12%. Research papers serve as the primary currency in academic research, enabling researchers to build upon existing knowledge and contribute new ideas. Unfortunately, current methods for summarizing research papers by reverse indexing or neural network-based approaches fail to provide a feasible means for non-experts to navigate the vast amount of academic literature easily. One promising solution to this problem involves developing a knowledge graph from indexed research papers that allows for natural language queries about scientific concepts, providing a more accessible pathway for users to explore the academic literature. In this research, we introduce a unique dataset, called QCR, consisting of both factual and open-ended questions that non-experts might pose when examining a knowledge graph of indexed research papers. For every question, a relevant research paper serves as the supporting fact, offering a means to evaluate the effectiveness of methods for constructing knowledge graphs and answering queries against them. The open-ended components of these questions, in turn, provide a basis for assessing the usefulness of such graphs for exploring the underlying research papers. One potential method for assessing the quality of these knowledge graphs is through the application of Inclusive Quality Metrics, acknowledging the importance of ensuring accessibility and inclusivity for all users. We demonstrate the utility of the QCR dataset by utilizing both machine learning and adversarial approaches to improve the performance of models evaluating the factuality of individual research paper assertions against the underlying research literature. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of utilizing pre-trained neural network-based models for both question answering and the generation of supporting research papers. Lastly, we explore the creation of a user interface that integrates both query answering and the generation of supporting research papers, providing a means for users to explore academic literature through natural language queries. In 2014, ASEP with velocity steps was proposed as a variant of the asymmetric simple exclusion process. This process involves additional exchanges where two particles swap places, effectively creating the illusion of particles moving at varying velocities. Our research extends this concept by examining the long-term behavior of ASEP with velocity steps in three distinct configurations: when particles can reach any velocity, when they are confined to only odd or only even velocities. Our findings show that in the former scenario, a phase transition occurs where particles eventually spread evenly throughout the system, whereas in the latter, particles remain confined to one side with probability directly correlated with the initial conditions. Additionally, we derive exact velocity distributions for all three cases and analyze how they relate to TASEP, the nearest-neighbor ASEP process. This research was initially presented as a part of the 2019 Mathematics Department at U.C. Berkeley's distinguished lecture series and is now being freely made available for public access. Due to copyright restrictions, permission is required before repurposing the associated figures. In our accompanying appendix, we correct an error found in the initial velocity distribution's derivation and provide an alternative path for proving exchange rate ratios for rate-1 ASEP step exchanges. These findings have since been applied to analysis of the TASEP speed process. In our revised study, we explore how these velocity exchanges impact the system's speed and particle density, in addition to releasing all attached supplementary material as part of this article. It has since been observed that these velocity exchanges can also result in particles becoming stuck together, forming a linked unit that moves as a single entity. Building on previous research, we predict not only initial conditions' steady-state distributions but also the equilibrium behavior of these bound particles. This bound particle model holds significant relevance as it directly relates to recent discoveries made on the ASEP speed process, whose underlying mechanism shares a striking similarity with the model presented here. With the model's generalizations, we are now able to freely explore various exclusion processes that incorporate multiple particles exchanging velocities simultaneously, and such extensions can be specifically applied to solve the fundamental question of whether an ASEP process can achieve a phase transition from an initial state that is not continuous to a continuous stationary state. This question holds immense significance because it is fundamentally intertwined with recent breakthroughs achieved on the ASEP speed process. Lastly, we provide a theoretical model that can be used to describe general exclusion processes and demonstrate that models based on this theory are analytically solvable. The properties of Dirac fermions are well characterized by their average behavior, which is often described by mean values and anticommutation relations. In contrast, this study focuses on linear Majorana fermions, which are unique particles that have the same wavefunction as their antiparticle. Unlike their half-linear counterparts, the anticharge operator does not satisfy a $c$-number susceptibility in the ground state. Instead, it maps the ground state to itself, indicating that the charge carries no information about the particle's position. As a result, the only accessible information about a linear Majorana fermion comes from the particle's charge and its pairing operator, which are linear combinations that represent the particle's location on two separate sites. The probability distribution of these combinations is not Gaussian, as evidenced by their skewness and kurtosis, which can be used as a distinguishing feature to identify Majorana fermions in a charge measurement. This phenomenon occurs because the distribution of the charge and its counterpart can be derived from each other, resulting in a symmetric, non-Gaussian distribution. Consequently, a linear Majorana fermion's signature in a charge measurement may be affected, particularly in systems where the particle's spatial distribution is measured under a discrete sampling process. This implies that anticharge measurements are inherently insufficient for identifying Majorana fermions. In contrast, our findings suggest that it may be possible to distinguish Majorana fermions from their counterparts using suitable, anticharge-based measurements. A linear Majorana fermion can also exhibit non-local effects, such as the influence of one particle's position on another's charge distribution, although this does not hold for the particle's location. Lastly, our study demonstrates that the unique statistical characteristics of a linear Majorana fermion can emerge even in a high-energy regime. This is because the distribution of the charge and its counterpart are determined by the particle's unique properties and its interaction with its surroundings, which dictate that only certain linear combinations of the particle's position can be described by a non-Gaussian distribution. As a result, a linear Majorana fermion's signature in a charge measurement may be unaffected by the particle's energy level. In conclusion, our study highlights the distinct statistical characteristics of linear Majorana fermions, which set them apart from their half-linear counterparts. This study investigates multiple advanced linear and nonlinear theory-based preconditioning techniques for a time integration method, specifically comparing their performance in scaling for a complex cardiac mechanics model. We examined various approaches, including Baliff-Bardin, Darvishkan, and nonlinear versions of Block-Lattice and Darvishkan methods, in both their embedded and standalone forms, against the classic Jacobi preconditioning technique. Our analysis spanned a range of problem sizes, from small to very large, encompassing hundreds to thousands of elements and numerous cardiac cells. We conducted our analysis both numerically with randomly generated data and experimentally using real cardiac mechanics data. Our findings show that the Baliff-Bardin and Block-Lattice preconditioners consistently outperform the classic Jacobi method across all scenarios. Although the Darvishkan and Kanemoto preconditioners demonstrate similar performance to the top performers in our analysis, they failed the scalability test with real data. Ultimately, this study provides a comprehensive evaluation of the performance of advanced preconditioning techniques for time integration methods on highly scalable cardiac mechanics simulations. As computational models of cardiac mechanics continue to grow in size, our analysis highlights the critical importance of selecting an appropriate preconditioning technique to leverage high-performance computing capabilities and achieve efficient solutions. The growing reliance on security protocols worldwide creates an environment where individuals can easily misinterpret the level of security being achieved. As a result, a significant threat emerges from the overconfidence that develops among those in charge, who are blinded by the superficial effectiveness of their security measures, ignoring the inherent flaws in modern security architecture that facilitate exploitation. In this paper, we explore the complex interplay between the increasing complexity of computer systems and the limitations of their users, examining how it gives rise to a perfect storm that is fueled by the escalating difficulty of maintaining security in today's technology-driven world. Ultimately, we must acknowledge that, regardless of advancements, computer systems will always have vulnerabilities that can be manipulated, and our goal as developers should be to accept and incorporate this reality into our design, recognizing that security is an ever-evolving concept. In this ever-evolving landscape, we must redefine our approach to security through a more realistic perspective that takes into account the inherent risks associated with modern computer systems and the limitations of their users. In this context, we introduce a new concept that quantifies the level of exploitation that can result from a security breach, referring to it as the "False Feeling of Safety" effect. This phenomenon occurs when users are misled by the appearance of security provided by traditional security protocols, such as encryption, key exchange, and digital signatures, and we demonstrate its financial implications through a new framework, highlighting the significant gains that can be achieved by cybercriminals who exploit these weaknesses. Furthermore, we examine several real-world attacks that illustrate the "False Feeling of Safety" effect in action and discuss potential countermeasures that can mitigate this phenomenon, and we conclude by outlining some directions for future research in this area. Despite significant research in reinforcement learning over the years, developing suitable methods for real-world problems has remained a challenge due to the lack of suitable evaluation tools and benchmarks. To address this issue, our work presents an novel, endless evaluation framework called L2Explorer, which leverages endless learning challenges to assess reinforcement learning algorithms on various task families defined by predefined attributes. This framework enables the creation of open-source challenges on unlimited grids, with infinite states, and we invite the community to collaborate with us on shaping the future of reinforcement learning in an endless evaluation setting. L2Explorer is currently applied to evaluate the performance of multiple state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms on diverse gridworld tasks. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/THU-OGC/L2Explorer, and we are excited to share this evaluation ecosystem with the community through our ongoing research. For more information on this project, please refer to the supplementary material accompanying this paper. To facilitate further discussion, a dedicated forum has been established at https://forum.rl-community.org/t/l2explorer-an- eternal-reinforcement-learning-evaluation-ecosystem/. Finally, we present L2Explorer at ICML 2023 as an extension to our previous work, EPEE, which was introduced at IJCAI 2023. For more details on our research, the reader is invited to review the accompanying presentation available at https://www.ogc.ai/publications/l2explorer. L2Explorer is an open-source project that is available under the permissive MIT License. To collaborate with us on this project, please reach out to us through an issue report on our GitHub repository. This approach also facilitates the identification of regions of the variable space that represent significant progress in process execution, thus enabling the detection of process instances making substantial progress. This innovation is then combined with a new distance metric that assesses the similarity between process instances, allowing for the declaration of processes that incorporate variables. This, in turn, enables the definition of regions of the variable space that should be monitored for process instances making progress. This is illustrated by a case study involving the monitoring of declarative processes, for which the proposed method offers improved performance compared to existing approaches. This method is part of a broader framework for the efficient monitoring of declarative processes and demonstrates its effectiveness through the integration of a case study and a technical comparison with existing methods. In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a localized state near the middle of a quasiperiodic arrangement, distant from the propagation's original and periodic crystal bases. This study employs a mathematical approach to investigate one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals and their interacting wave modes. By applying a tight-binding model and a Fourier-space approach, our researchers reveal the intricate relationship between the quasiperiodic arrangement's characteristics and the delocalized state, observing a previously unpredicted effect where a shift from localization to delocalization occurs as the quasiperiodic features become more distinct. This phenomenon is shown to result from the interplay between two competing influences: the scattering of waves by quasiperiodic variations and their attempts to maintain long-range order. This finding is demonstrated through both numerical simulations and a theoretical analysis, providing a clearer understanding of this wave propagation phenomenon. This knowledge can be applied across fields to explain and predict the behavior of waves in quasiperiodic structures in one-dimensional settings. This study also presents a method for calculating the delocalized state shift, which can be adapted to analyze other low-energy properties in one-dimensional quasiperiodic systems. By modifying a one-dimensional quasicrystal array to a two-dimensional bi-directional quasicrystal, this research reveals that the delocalized state shift may be a more general occurrence and can be influenced by the wave's direction of propagation. This realization offers a potential approach to managing the delocalized state shift in two-dimensional quasiperiodic systems by adjusting the wave's direction of propagation. This study provides a deeper understanding of wave propagation in one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures and may provide a means to control the delocalized state shift in two-dimensional quasiperiodic systems by modifying the wave's direction of propagation. This could have implications for designing and optimizing two-dimensional quasiperiodic structures that utilize wave propagation, such as photonic quasicrystals, phononic quasicrystals, and graphene quasicrystals, to achieve the optimal localization or delocalization of waves and modes. This knowledge can also be applied to other one-dimensional quasiperiodic systems by modifying the model to match the specific characteristics of the system in question. In our research, we explored the capabilities of spatial mode demultiplexing (SMD) using bi-photon beams generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, and found that these beams exhibit an unusual property - when they are split into two separate photons, they can provide a level of super-resolution beyond what is theoretically achievable with a single photon. This phenomenon arises due to the entangled state of the photons, and we demonstrated that their combined signal allows for the distinction between spatial modes that, when separated, are too close to differentiate with a single photon. As a result, we were able to successfully demultiplex two closely spaced Gaussian modes that, when examined individually, could not be distinguished. This achievement has significant implications for the development of future optical communication systems that can process high-channel-count signals. Furthermore, our research revealed that the super-resolution effect can be achieved even with photons that are not highly correlated, provided that they originate from a source that is capable of producing narrow spectral mode spacing. This finding provides a more flexible approach to SMD, allowing for the use of broader spectral sources that are more readily available. Overall, our study has the potential to contribute to the advancement of source-side spatial mode multiplexing and demultiplexing technologies. Additionally, we have also examined the potential of our system for error correction in optical communication systems. As a source of bi-photon spatial mode pairs can be highly redundant, our research may offer a path to enhancing the capacity of optical communication systems through source engineering. Lastly, we have explored the feasibility of extending our proof-of-concept to other types of spatial modes using numerical modeling, and our results indicate that our approach can be applied to demultiplexing modes such as Laguerre-Gaussian modes and bessel modes. As such, our research provides a foundation for investigating a broader range of spatial mode structures. This work proposes a novel approach to understanding the nature of singularities in algebraic and analytic geometric spaces by drawing from the principles of modern algebraic geometry and the legacy of René Thom's theory for differentiable manifolds. The foundation of this approach is the concept of a formal function as a coefficient for analytic germs, enabling the representation of spaces like $\mathbb{A}^n_k$ and $k^n$ through a set of points defined by equations and relationships. The focus then shifts to investigating the properties of spaces like orbits under group actions, by examining how they are constructed and the role of Schur polynomials in such constructions. An example of this is provided by considering the space of surfaces in $\mathbb{A}^3_k$. The proposed approach also offers a framework for connecting geometric spaces to the combinatorial structure of faces in vector spaces. The relationship between spaces defined over fields and their equivalent definitions in monoids is also explored, along with the resulting generalizations to spaces defined over fields with valuation structures. The paper concludes by discussing the potential for applying this approach to study spaces in the context of modern homotopy theory. In dynamic ecosystems, population demographics undergo significant and temporary changes, affecting the behavior of interacting species and ultimately the ecosystem as a whole. However, identifying the distinct patterns of short-lived fluctuations and distinguishing them from significant, prolonged shifts in the ecosystem is crucial. This research aims to establish a framework for examining transient and lasting changes in ecosystem behavior by introducing a relative distance metric to map ecosystem paths and utilizing it in conjunction with a neighbor graph to classify the duration of transients and shifts. We apply this framework to data from a predator-prey ecosystem with intrinsic daily and annual cycles, accurately identifying transient and lasting changes and potential early indicators of significant shifts in the ecosystem. Notably, our analysis reveals distinct patterns in ecosystem behavior at different time scales, highlighting the importance of considering the ecosystem's bi-timescales when analyzing demographic changes. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that in complex ecosystems like the one studied, a measure of relative distance can effectively capture the ecosystem's dynamics across different time scales. This work paves the way for the exploration of the ecosystem's behavior in response to external influences and the development of early warning systems for significant changes in ecosystems. Additionally, our study's methods can be adapted to analyze and predict the behavior of other complex systems that exhibit transient and lasting changes. This research is an initial step towards a broader exploration of the ecosystem's behavior and the development of predictive models, and it is expected to contribute to the advancement of fields like nonlinear science, ecology, and network science. Furthermore, our study's findings can be applied to other areas like sociology, medicine, and climate science, and the proposed early alert indicators and warning systems can be used to inform policy decisions and management strategies in ecosystems and other complex systems. Our analysis reveals a marked distinction in the distribution of bulge-to-total stellar mass ratios in galaxies with elevated mass. Furthermore, when excluding low-probability outliers, there exists a distinct, tight 1-to-1 relationship between star formation rates and stellar masses in both disk-dominated and bulge-dominated galaxy populations. However, since even low-probability outliers hold considerable statistical significance, it is essential to investigate their characteristics. Our research indicates that multi-task learning models can effectively generalize sentiment patterns across languages, with significant performance gains in low-resource languages. Furthermore, we discover that, within a task, the similarity between languages has a positive impact on performance, with performance peaking at around 50% linguistic similarity. In efforts to address global challenges through individual actions, the concept of self-control via self-reinforcement and self-penalty has been extensively studied. However, these models typically assume a fixed action cost, neglecting variations in an agent's ability, a crucial aspect when scaling to large societies. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new model where agents can choose between two types of control mechanisms: one involving a certain self-reinforcing effect and a guaranteed penalty, or a probabilistic penalty with potential benefits. We demonstrate that in a stylized economy with heterogeneous agents and an infinite time horizon, the optimal control mechanism is one where the probability of self-penalty is a function of the agent's type, reflecting a level of self-disapproval. When applied to a global public good problem, our model facilitates a more efficient social outcome than previous self-control models. Notably, our results also indicate that in certain cases, a social Doleman effect may emerge, where the social welfare is actually lower when individuals face higher personal costs of control. We validate our theoretical findings with a corresponding laboratory experiment. The study reveals that when the probability of self-penalty is hidden, players tend to choose the guaranteed penalty approach, but with the cost revealed, they select the probabilistic penalty with potential benefits. Interestingly, when the cost is framed as a loss rather than a gain, players' preferences reverse, mirroring the predicted self-disapproval effect. The results also show that individual self-control choices deviate from predicted optimal levels, attributed to a self-confirmation bias. The study further explores how the effect of self-reinforcement and self-penalty interact with each other, finding that players tend to choose strategies that maximize their self-reinforcement but only up to a certain point, beyond which the cost of control dominates. The research also delves into the impact of different social interactions on subjects' decision-making, but interestingly, no significant variations were observed across treatment conditions. The results do, however, suggest that in distribution games, players exhibit a more complex decision-making process, one that is influenced by multiple factors, making it challenging to identify a clear pattern. In 2019, Li and Prendiville refined this to state that if A and B produce no more than 4 unique elements and A is larger than G, then the intersection of A and B is greater than 2/3 of A. Here, we further expand on this by showing that under the 4 distinct element condition, A and B can overlap by a rate of at least 7/10. Additionally, we provide a lower bound of 9/11 for pairs of sets that do not necessarily form a group. Furthermore, we provide a method for solving the 3k-4 conjecture by reducing it to a smaller, nearly equivalent problem. Finally, an intuitive approach to Freiman's 2k-2 conjecture is also outlined.

This research paper addresses the unexplored area of fractional Brownian motion (fBm) with a specific drift value. We investigate the nature of Borel sets within $\mathbb{R}^d$, particularly those that result in a non-empty interior when combined with the standard Lebesgue measure and shifted by a given drift $b$. Our analysis also delves into identifying the smallest possible measures, denoted as $\tau(b)$, that give those Borel sets an interior. Furthermore, when $d$ is greater than one, we prove that almost every drift value $b$ leads to a measure $\tau(b)$ equal to zero. However, when $d$ is equal to one, we discover that all measures $\tau(b)$ are positive. Additionally, we establish that, regardless of the dimension, all measures $\tau(b)$ are continuous. Building upon existing work by T. J. Lyons on the conditional expectation of fBms, we leverage the concept of cascade repleteness to demonstrate that, for all $d$ greater than one, all measures $\tau(b)$ are strictly positive. Finally, we discuss implications of our findings on the structure of fBms with fixed drifts.

This construction upholds the principle of simplicial minimality, allowing us to express the global simplicial bundle as an equivalent simplicial structure consisting of local components over the simplicial category. These components are obtained by applying the functor category framework to the category of simplices within $X$. This method generalizes a previous approach developed for simplicial groups. Furthermore, we utilize this principle to establish a connection between global simplicial bundles and simplicial action groups. This relationship is particularly reflected in the category framework, revealing that the global simplicial bundle is equivalent to the category of simplicial action groups. This paper proposes novel design approaches for Golay complementary structures in multiple frequency bands. By applying a specific transformation to a pair of complementary functions, we derive pairs of periodic functions with complementary autocorrelation properties. We then develop even and odd symmetry criteria for these functions to create symmetric patterns with zero cross-correlation. A set of quadrature mirror filter (QMF) pairs can be obtained from these symmetric patterns. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by designing QMF pairs in hexagonal and square layouts for BPSK signals. Our designs outperform existing multi-carrier QMF structures in cross-correlation performance, and can be readily extended to larger Golay codes. Notably, our designs require significantly fewer subcarriers than existing extensions of multi-carrier QMF structures. We also explore the applicability of our approach to larger Golay codes and discuss potential design flaws. Our designs exhibit superior performance in multiuser detection scenarios. Furthermore, we investigate the performance of our designs when subjected to phase shifts and carrier frequency offsets. Our results suggest that the improved cross-correlation properties of our designs can lead to significant gains in BER, with gains of up to 2.5 dB in some cases. We also examine the spectral efficiency of our designs and propose methods for optimizing subcarrier allocation. Our designs can be readily implemented using existing multi-carrier QMF structures with minimal modifications. We provide numerical examples of subcarrier allocations for different numbers of subcarriers and demonstrate the applicability of our designs to large Golay codes. Our designs can be extended to other modulation schemes such as 16-QAM, and we provide design parameters for these schemes. We investigate the potential of our designs to be applied to other fields such as sensor arrays and imaging systems, and propose the term multi-carrier complementary structures for our designs. We also explore the historical development of Golay complementary structures and provide a perspective on the field. We discuss potential research directions for multi-carrier complementary structures, and propose methods for optimizing the cross-correlation properties of these structures. We examine the statistical properties of our designs and propose methods for analyzing their performance. We investigate the long-term performance of our designs and propose methods for predicting their behavior. We discuss the challenges of implementing our designs in practice, and propose methods for mitigating these challenges. We investigate the feasibility of our designs for large Golay codes, and propose methods for implementing these designs efficiently. This connection is particularly evident when considering the graded ring formed by the intersection and union of these partitions, which relates to the graded ring constructed from elements of a simplicial ring. Our exploration of this analogy leads us to define a sequence of integers for any simplicial ring and discuss the underlying properties of its associated graded ring, expanding on the ideas presented in a preceding preprint. Furthermore, we expand on the idea that the graded ring can be seen as a collection of counting partitions with respect to a specific ordering, which is determined by a simplicial version of the dimension function. This dimension function is utilized in developing a geometric interpretation of the graded ring, which is analogous to but distinct from the geometry underlying the original set of integers. This distinction gives rise to different division ring-related constructs, which in turn lead to generalized versions of the Nilpotent depth and the ring's dimension, both of which have previously been referred to as the'simplicial dimension'. We also examine how these constructs behave when the underlying ring is altered from being simplicial to being 'non-simplicial'. This transformation is essentially equivalent to altering the order in which the ring's components are considered, which in turn changes the associated counting partitions and their resulting properties. This change of order can lead to distinct, potentially nilpotent elements appearing as non-nilpotent when considering the order of the simplicial ring, which in turn gives rise to a distinction in the way we define and operate on simplicial rings in comparison to their non-simplicial counterparts. This difference in order also results in a variation in how we define and apply homotopy theory-related constructs to simplicial rings, which in turn may lead to different, additional simplicial types of elements and their associated properties, which in turn may not be captured by a simplicial construct. We establish a more general framework applicable to any partially ordered set with a specific property and provide examples of such sets, which in turn enable us to define a broader sequence of integers that encompasses the previously mentioned divisibility sequences, which in turn enables us to generalize previous theorems and provide new insights on the underlying structure of homotopy theory. Securing communication and coordination of these astrobots is crucial as even minor vulnerabilities could compromise data integrity and threaten the success of the mission. We conducted a comprehensive security evaluation by simulating the SDSS-V system and identifying potential threats in its protocol, followed by a formal security verification using a tool that guarantees the protocol's security based on a given set of security properties. This evaluation leverages the latest advancements in timing and fault tolerance research, ensuring that even astrobots with different clock settings, suffering from delays and failures, can securely coordinate and synchronize their actions. Additionally, we implemented and tested this secure protocol on a small-scale SDSS-V system consisting of three astrobots, using a combination of simulated and real-world environments. The results demonstrate that this protocol ensures the integrity and confidentiality of data and meets the SDSS-V system's performance requirements, even in the presence of timing attacks and failures. Moreover, this protocol exhibits a high level of responsiveness and energy efficiency, achieving a data secure and timely completion in 93% of cases within the designated 24-hour timeframe. General Purpose processors possess the capability to execute a wide range of tasks efficiently, making them inherently adaptable and capable of tackling diverse problems. However, despite being universally applicable, general purpose processors are consistently outperformed by specialized hardware components that are designed to handle particular functions, often through the use of custom hardware components that match the problem's structure. This disparity in performance is attributed to the unique design of GP processors, which are constructed with a variety of functions in mind but fail to optimize performance for any single operation. As a result, the GP compiler is required to manually adjust the processor's configuration to optimize performance for a specific function by activating specific parts of the processor. This requirement has given birth to the GP compiler, a type of hardware that combines a variety of general-purpose cores on a single chip and is capable of reconfiguring itself to execute different instructions simultaneously. Nevertheless, the full potential of such compilers remains unrealized due to the constraint of control data, which restricts the compiler's ability to fully utilize the available core resources, resulting in less than optimal performance. In order to overcome this limitation, the Enhanced GP 2 compiler is proposed, incorporating an innovative new method for issuing instructions that is free from control data, allowing for the creation of more complex and efficient patterns of execution that are capable of fully leveraging the capabilities of the available core resources. As a result, this compiler is capable of generating performance that is comparable to that of custom hardware components, while also being easily adaptable to a wide range of applications with minimal modifications to the core, and is therefore the most optimal solution for a wide range of problem domains. Furthermore, the proposed method for issuing instructions is also adaptable to GP graphs, allowing for the easy execution of a wide range of algorithms, and is therefore the most suitable and efficient compiler for a wide range of applications. In order to verify the performance of the Enhanced GP 2 compiler, a custom hardware component was designed using a GP processor, and the results showed that the proposed method for issuing instructions is capable of achieving performance that is up to 3 times better than custom hardware components for certain applications, and is therefore the most optimal solution for a wide range of problem domains. In order to further validate the performance of the Enhanced GP 2 compiler, a custom hardware component was designed using a GP processor, and the results showed that the proposed method for issuing instructions is capable of achieving performance that is up to 3 times better than custom hardware components for certain applications, and is therefore the most optimal solution for a wide range of problem domains

The attribute extraction task in computer vision involves linking text labels to specific visual features. A common approach uses a separate model for each attribute and a classifier for each corresponding text label, but this can be costly due to the large number of attributes and labels. An alternative is to use a unified model for all attributes and labels, but this requires a significant amount of annotated data for each one, which is often difficult to obtain. In this paper, we present a novel unified model that utilizes a dual-path structure for attribute extraction, leveraging both domain-specific and domain-agnostic information for each attribute. By using a separate branch for each attribute, it extracts features unique to that feature, while using a shared branch for all attributes allows the model to capture general features that are present across the domain. Additionally, we employ a contrastive learning loss function to refine the model's predictions and reduce the distance between similar visual features. Our unified model outperforms existing attribute extraction methods that use separate models and achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods that use separate models for each attribute while significantly reducing the number of model parameters. Notably, our model achieves a mean average precision (AP) of 0.354 on the ANKI dataset, surpassing the previous best reported result by a significant margin of 0.013%, while using only 0.38% of the parameters of the previous best reported result. Our model also demonstrates strong performance on the VREID dataset, achieving a mean AP of 0.321, the highest among all published methods. Recently, Yeo and Kwon introduced the concept of normal quotient networks within the context of twisted graphs. Building upon their work, we expand upon their findings by presenting a novel infinite series of star normal quotient networks that are of the twisted wreath type. Our presentation includes specific examples of graphs $\Gamma$ whose normal quotients correspond to star twisted wreath graphs connected to central vertices, with particular examples being infinite collections of star normal quotient networks of the twisted wreath type. Furthermore, we provide a general formula for the parameter $k$ in the star twisted wreath graph $\Gamma_n^{(k)}$. Recent advances in large language models have shown impressive performance in various tasks, outperforming human competition in some cases. However, the significant disparity between the number of processed training samples and real-world interactions makes their general knowledge limited to just their training data. To bridge this knowledge gap, we propose introducing structured knowledge from existing sources, such as text databases and ontologies, to augment these models through structured inference. This approach, called SKILL, leverages diverse knowledge bases to enable extensive language models to accurately answer a wide range of questions, encompassing not only factual questions but also those requiring common sense, categorization, and inference. By incorporating a question-question similarity measure and a knowledge inference framework, SKILL seamlessly addresses both simple and complex queries, even those with multiple hops of inference. In our experiments, we show that SKILL successfully enhances the performance of these models on diverse tasks, including natural language understanding, by incorporating various knowledge bases such as Wikipedia, WordNet, and DBpedia. For instance, our results indicate that the models' overall NLU accuracy can be elevated to 79.5% (+3.5% absolute) when trained with the SKILL framework. Furthermore, we explore the effect of various knowledge bases on different NLU tasks, opening up avenues for further research in the interplay between models, data, and tasks. However, determining the optimal angle for these shots is not immediately clear due to varying environmental factors such as outdoor lighting and indoor layout. This problem is significant enough that some 360-degree camera systems adjust their shooting direction based on user input. This paper presents two novel approaches for automatically determining the preferred angle for these shots, regardless of whether it's based on an aesthetic standard or another consideration, such as minimizing shadows. These methods involve analyzing the overlap region between consecutive photos and evaluating various features of the scene, and they are tested on a range of scenarios to measure their effectiveness in producing high-quality stitched images. The result is that these methods can produce stitched images that are indistinguishable from those created with the full range of shot angles, as determined by both a automated quality assessment tool and human subjects. The techniques also prove adaptable to different input data, such as light fields and depth maps, that can be used to incorporate additional factors that affect the preferred angle. This study develops a biophysical model of the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) neurons in marmoset monkeys to explain the neuronal dysfunction underlying Parkinson's disease. The brain region SNpc is responsible for producing the neurotransmitter dopamine, which is depleted in patients with Parkinson's, leading to severe motor disorders. To create the model, we employed a computational framework that incorporates multiple ion channels to accurately replicate the electrical behavior of neurons. The model includes a population of cholinergic interneurons that uses the Wang-Buszaki 2006 model and a set of striatal neurons that uses the Amari 1977 model to generate excitatory and inhibitory inputs, respectively. The model also accounts for the effects of excessive acetylcholine released by cholinergic interneurons in individuals with Parkinson's. Our computational model uses a reduced set of Hodgkin-Huxley-type neuron models and a range of ion channels, specifically including a persistent sodium current, which is thought to contribute to the generation of action potential bursts in SNpc neurons. In our model, we simulate the effects of deep brain stimulation (DBS) on an SNpc network by applying an electric current to mimic the therapeutic benefits of this treatment. Our results suggest that both low-frequency and high-frequency DBS can restore normal firing patterns in SNpc neurons by controlling the release of acetylcholine. Our data also indicate that high-frequency DBS has a more lasting impact on the model's neurons. Our research provides a framework for investigating the treatment of Parkinson's disease using computational models. In future studies, we plan to develop a larger-scale computational model of the basal ganglia to explore its implications in Parkinson's disease. Furthermore, we aim to examine the effects of DBS in this larger model and explore potential new approaches to treating the disorder. We propose a novel DPCRN model to enhance individual speech channels in a mixture of sounds. This model leverages two unique components: a convolutional layer to extract general characteristics from all channels, and a recurrent layer to analyze each channel's specific properties. Through dual paths, DPCRN integrates the information from both components, allowing for more effective suppression of background noise and interference. Experimental results show that our model achieves superior performance compared to existing methods in various metrics. Specifically, DPCRN outperforms existing techniques in terms of distortion, noise reduction, and overall speech quality, as evidenced by lower PESQ, SDR, and COMPLEXITY scores. Furthermore, DPCRN's performance is on par with state-of-the-art multi-channel techniques like DDF-DPC and MC-ASSA while requiring significantly fewer parameters. Our model's parameters total around 185,000, in contrast to around 2,500,000 parameters in DDF-DPC and MC-ASSA. Additionally, DPCRN exhibits competitive performance in the 1,024-channel case, suggesting its potential as a scalable solution for large-channel counts. We examined how modified $f(R)$ gravity and heavy neutroscale dark fields in High-Scale Higgs Portal Standard Model affect the turn-around radii of dark matter structures, using a simple, analytical model. By considering a range of neutrino masses (up to a few GeV) and Higgs portal couplings (from very weak to weak), we determined the corresponding scale of the turn-around radius. Our results indicate that large neutrino masses or Higgs portal couplings significantly alter the turn-around radii, making them much larger than predicted by the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. We discovered that for certain combinations of these modifications, the turn-around radii could be comparable to or even larger than the virial radii, potentially offering a more straightforward explanation for the observed discrepancies between $\Lambda$CDM and $f(R)$ gravity in galaxy clusters. Furthermore, we found that heavy neutrinos or Higgs portal couplings can alleviate the tension between the predicted and observed masses of galaxy clusters, particularly in the case of massive clusters like Coma. However, we also found that these modifications cannot entirely resolve the conflict between $\Lambda$CDM and $f(R)$ gravity in cluster scaling relations. Notably, we found that while a 1 eV right-handed neutrino can resolve the mass discrepancy in galaxy clusters, a 1 GeV right-handed neutrino would result in overproduction of solars, an inconsistency with existing observations. Finally, we found that turn-around radii can provide valuable constraints on the parameters of modified gravity theories, particularly when combined with other observational data, such as the abundance of galaxy clusters, which can yield a minimum 95% confidence interval of $M_\nu \gtrsim 0.4$ GeV or $k_\phi \gtrsim 10^{-11}$, depending on the other parameter. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS upgrade for the upcoming High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC), a new generation of silicon pixel sensors is being developed to enhance the detector's capacity to handle elevated luminosity levels. Although the initially planned production pixel detector prototype prototypes have been constructed and tested, we have undertaken a comprehensive examination of the reconstructed track data from the first set of phase-one prototype blades in order to evaluate their performance. These prototypes, built around the time of the 2009 LHC shutdown, feature a 3D silicon pixel detector design with a thin 640-micron readout layer. We have examined jet and vertex reconstruction results obtained from 7 TeV proton-proton collision data, also reviewing the reliability of the 2009 hit reconstruction software for reference. Our study incorporates detailed 3D hit information to enhance track and vertex finding, in line with the upgraded detector design. We have investigated the precision of vertex position determination, primary vertex finding efficiency, and jet reconstruction using 12-16 of the 18 planned forward pixel blades. Our findings contribute to the validation of the CMS pixel detector's upgraded design and provide valuable insights for the design of future detector components. Furthermore, these results are significant in the broader context of the ongoing development of silicon tracking systems in various particle physics experiments. Additionally, they highlight the importance of ongoing prototyping efforts in the field prior to the start of data collection during the HL-LHC era. In late 2016, a second set of larger-scale prototype blades became available, featuring larger active areas and better readout layers, and we have undertaken additional jet and vertex reconstruction studies with these newer prototypes using 50 c/fb of 13 TeV proton-proton collision data. Our new results demonstrate improved performance, in line with extrapolated findings from previous studies. In this presentation, we will provide a comprehensive overview of both sets of results. In particular, we will be reviewing in-depth track and vertex reconstruction data obtained from 7 TeV and 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, also examining the enhanced performance of the upgraded detector design. related tweets together into sentiment categories.
An LSTM-based model is developed for the primary task of individual tweet classification,
while a neural network model is introduced for the secondary task of sentiment classification
on a aggregated tweet collection.
The proposed LSTM model is systematically optimized and its performance evaluated against
multiple competitors using a comprehensive dataset consisting of 50,000 classified tweets.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged Anti-de Sitter black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an independent probe of black hole phase transitions. We further explore this by linking the thermal entropy of a nonlinear, charged Anti-de Sitter black hole to its shadow radius, providing evidence that this connection is consistent with the holographic principle. Ultimately, we establish that the shadow radius of a black hole can serve as a thermal probe, offering a non-intrusive means of determining both local and non-local thermal properties. This insight can be applied to a broad class of black holes that exhibit phase transitions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the thermal entropy of a nonlinear, charged Anti-de Sitter black hole is equivalent to the shadow entropy, which is defined as the entropy associated with the shadow radius. This definition can be applied to a broad class of black holes that exhibit thermal fluctuations, providing a unified framework for studying both local and non-local thermal behavior. This framework can also be used to investigate the thermal fluctuations of black holes that do not have a well-defined horizon, such as those described by the Membranary gravitational theory of General relativity. Furthermore, we show that the thermal entropy of a nonlinear, charged Anti-de Sitter black hole can exhibit non-integer dimensions, providing evidence for the holographic principle. This principle is supported by the fact that the thermal entropy of a nonlinear, charged Anti-de Sitter black hole is proportional to the shadow radius to the power of (d/2), which is consistent with the holographic conjecture. This relationship can be expressed as $S \propto R_s^{d/2}$, which is a universal law that applies to a broad class of black holes that exhibit thermal fluctuations. This universal law can be used to determine the thermal entropy of a black hole based on its shadow radius, providing a non-intrusive means of accessing this information.

While both aspects are crucial, there is currently a lack of research that simultaneously addresses both in the context of quantum state tomography. This study fills this gap by exploring both entanglement and synchronization in the tomographic representation of a two-mode state, examining how they are interlinked and how they are affected by different statistical analysis methods. Our research reveals that while there is no universal agreement on the non-classical nature of a state across all tomographic projections, there is always a consensus on the presence of synchronized behavior. Furthermore, we found that the degree of synchronization can be a more sensitive indicator of the system's complexity than the degree of entanglement. Our findings also highlight the importance of employing manifestly orthogonal tomographic projections to accurately analyze both entanglement and synchronization. This approach offers a more precise understanding of the relationship between these aspects and the effects of different analysis methods, providing valuable insights for the study of open quantum systems and non-destructive state measurement. Through this study, we demonstrate that both entanglement and synchronization play a vital role in the description of quantum states, and that their interlinkage is a fundamental aspect that must be considered in any analysis. This research is particularly relevant to the study of quantum applications, such as quantum communication and metrology, where the presence of synchronized states is a critical factor. Our results also highlight the significance of choosing the appropriate reconstruction method, as this can either preserve or compromise the quantum properties of interest, underscoring the significance of methodological research in this field. Ultimately, this study offers a new perspective on the analysis of quantum states, emphasizing the importance of considering both entanglement and synchronization in order to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the underlying dynamics. This insight is equally applicable to the study of classical systems exhibiting complex behavior, as the concepts of synchronization and entanglement are equally relevant in these contexts. This study provides a foundation for further exploration into the interlinkage of these concepts across different state representations, as well as the effects of different reconstruction methods on the emergent properties of these systems. Controlling the spread of disease in plant systems is an complex task, involving multiple variables that compete for limited resources. Understanding the underlying dynamics of this process requires significant mathematical modeling efforts. In the case of fungal diseases on trees, such as strawberry plants, a simple model has proven effective in predicting the spread of disease using a reaction-diffusion system with a variational approach. However, this model falls short when applied to open systems like tree networks, as it fails to account for the continuous release of spores. The growing popularity of 360-degree (360°) video viewing is providing an engaging way for travelers to explore destinations. However, current 360° video viewing methods, which allow users to navigate freely, can be overwhelming and may lead to viewer fatigue. To address this issue, this research introduces an innovative approach, called viewport forecasting, which predicts user viewing navigation within a 360° video. Specifically, our proposed method, subtitle-driven viewport forecasting, utilizes subtitles as supplementary navigation information to predict user viewing navigation. Through both human and artificial evaluations, our approach demonstrated significant improvements over baseline methods, confirming the valuable role of subtitles in enhancing viewport prediction accuracy. Notably, our research showcases the practical benefits of subtitle-driven viewport forecasting by integrating our approach into an interactive user interface, enabling efficient 360° video traversal and viewing experience. Furthermore, our study provides insights into the underlying factors influencing user navigation within a 360° video, aided by visual analytics and statistical correlations. Ultimately, our findings contribute valuable insights to viewport forecasting, a crucial aspect for the travel and media industries, and pave the way for further research into the underlying user navigation patterns. Our research is also accompanied by an interactive demo, accessible at https://subtitle-360-forecast.net/, allowing users to explore and experience our viewport forecasting approach. This research is a initial exploration into viewport forecasting for 360° travel video, and we anticipate that future studies will investigate additional aspects, including user engagement and overall viewing experience. In this study, we examine k-strong shortest path covers in specific graphs, such as trees, planar graphs, and grids, as well as in general networks, with the additional constraint that the start and end nodes of each path must be distinct. Theoretical upper and lower bounds for the number of required k-strong shortest paths were derived for these graph types, with specific general network conditions. This research also validates the effectiveness of a heuristic algorithm designed to solve k-strong shortest path cover problems efficiently. The results show that this heuristic can generate high-quality solutions close to the optimal, with an average coverage rate of over 90% for the tested instances. The code for this research is openly available on GitHub. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of strong shortest path covers in networks and provide practical solutions for covering all nodes with a strong k-path. The study covers a range of real-world applications, including delivering software updates over networks and optimizing vehicle routes in delivery networks. One of the main challenges in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) is selecting the optimal output word from a vast vocabulary. Current methods, such as the softmax function, resolve this issue by assigning a probability to each possible word but suffer from slow convergence and poor performance. In contrast, our proposed approach draws from reinforcement learning to address this problem, leveraging a learning signal to directly evaluate the quality of each output word. To efficiently process extensive action spaces, we introduce a word-level mask to circumvent repeated token embeddings computations. By integrating our approach into the standard NMT framework, we achieve significant improvements in speed and efficiency without compromising performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms softmax by a substantial margin on NMT metrics and reduces training time by approximately 2 times for large vocabulary datasets. Furthermore, our approach surpasses the performance of softmax+noise by 0.17 in BLEU score at a 10 times faster training speed. We also observe that our method's effectiveness is vocabulary-size independent and delivers consistent improvements in data size experiments. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/rmt. In particular, our proposed model achieves a BLEU score of 32.15 on the IWSLT2017 De-En test set, a 0.39-point improvement over the standard NMT model. Moreover, with a word-level action space, our method delivers a 4.17-point BLEU score gain without decreasing training speed. We anticipate our work to contribute positively to the exploration of numerous action spaces encountered in other sequence-generation tasks. The growing interest in developing and utilizing vast medical image collections for training models has led to a significant issue: many practitioners are recreating existing datasets by annotating previously labeled images, essentially a form of image relabeling. In this research, we focus on identifying intrinsic prejudices in these annotated data, which refers to the discrepancy in annotations when comparing pairs of similar images, unless the difference is based on objective features like age, gender, or health conditions. Contrary to previous beliefs, the pressure within the cavity is found to be greater than the critical density of the universe, allowing for the persistence of a shock wave. Finally, our study demonstrates that the cavity's pressure can be measured through the analysis of Damped Oscillations. This understanding of first-blast shock waves provides valuable insights for future cosmological studies. Furthermore, our findings suggest a need to reevaluate previous models, particularly those related to Damped Oscillations, to incorporate the effects of an expanding universe. Lastly, our study shows that the universe's current state lies within a regime where the solution is governed by the combination of an expanding universe and a spherical cavity, rather than a regime dominated by a shock wave-driven universe. This has significant implications for the universe's early stages, indicating that the inner cavity's pressure should be considered when modeling such periods. This implies that the universe's early, rapidly changing phases should be reevaluated with this new pressure perspective. Our investigation uncovered an unseen acoustic phenomenon associated with adhesive strip shedding, often described as a "crackling" sound. Initially, this sound was thought to originate from the mechanical interaction between the shedding edge and the air stream it creates. However, our results reveal that this sound actually comes from a different source - specific patterns forming on the adhesive strip as it sheds. These patterns, comprised of isolated islands of adhesion, fragment into varying shapes, producing a diverse range of frequencies of the "crackling" sound. Interestingly, the frequencies of these patterns fall into distinct categories or "octaves," separated by a consistent frequency ratio of approximately 1.19. This unique, universally applicable ratio is a fundamental attribute of the shedding edge's geometry and movement. It remains constant across different air stream velocities and sheddable materials, offering a fundamental understanding of this peculiar acoustic phenomenon. This newfound insight also enables the prediction of specific frequency components of the "crackling" sound, shedding further light on the intricate yet universally applicable mechanics underlying this intriguing sound. This "crackling" sound, a seemingly random acoustic phenomenon, has been broken down into its precise constitutional elements, offering a groundbreaking understanding of its underlying mechanics. This unique acoustic experience, a combination of non-linear mechanical interactions and unique patterns of adhesion, fragmenting into diverse shapes and producing distinct frequencies of sound, has the capacity to serve as a model for exploring other complex acoustic phenomena. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic deepfake media necessitates the immediate development of an effective deepfake detection methodology. Although numerous algorithms have been proposed in recent years, the majority of them rely on facial region templates and, more critically, predominantly address the challenge from a single-domain perspective, namely, the detection of deepfakes within a specific domain, be it video or image. In contrast, our proposed framework, MD-CSDNetwork, a multi-domain cross-sewn network, tackles the deepfake detection issue on an equal footing with both media types and across multiple domains. In particular, we introduce a novel dual-sew network approach that simultaneously trains two types of training data with distinct temporal characteristics, namely, sequence-based data and individual-sample-based data. Furthermore, in line with best practices in feature extraction, our proposed framework includes two additional minor modifications, namely, the incorporation of a pre-trained visual back-bone and the employment of a score function to enhance performance. Across three comprehensive benchmark datasets, namely, FaceForeniscII++, Deepfake Detection Dataset, and Sony Deepfake Dataset, MD-CSDNetwork exhibits superior or on-par performance in comparison to the current state-of-the-art domain-specific methods at the time of our literature review. Moreover, our methodology boasts high consistency in both domain-specific and generalisable performance, as evidenced by comprehensive domain-ablation experiments and cross-domain evaluation results. The primary aim of this study is to analyze how the distribution of link degrees in DDL LDPC codes influences their error-correction capabilities when the BEC is known at the decoder. Moreover, this research demonstrates that the degree-degree linked ensemble (DDLE) performance is equivalent to that of regular LDPC ensembles when the BEC is known at the decoder. In 1930, Karl Menger introduced the concept of an n-dimensional angle space for n greater than or equal to one. He then posed several questions regarding the topological properties of these spaces. We provide answers to two of his unanswered questions: whether a one-dimensional angle space is homeomorphic to the standard one-dimensional Euclidean space, and whether a two-dimensional angle space can be homeomorphically mapped onto the standard two-dimensional Euclidean space. Our proof also demonstrates that any dimension greater than two allows for homeomorphic mappings between Euclidean space and angle space. This resolution to Menger's questions originates from a previous work by Menger in 1927 on the concept of order types. This connection is utilized to offer a simpler solution than the one initially provided by J. R. Shoenfield in 1983. Furthermore, this proof facilitates an exploration of general order types for spaces with specific dimensions. Additionally, this research extends to so-called semi-angle spaces, which are related to but distinct from standard angle spaces. This distinction leads to additional unresolved questions regarding the topological properties of these spaces. This work is also applicable to spaces defined using certain binary relations, which are a subject of current research in the field of topology. This includes specific spaces such as the space resulting from a binary relation that is both cyclic and connected, and the standard two-dimensional Euclidean space, which can be mapped onto an eight-dimensional angle space. Research indicates that living organisms can detect and respond to various environmental patterns, including those that are neutral in composition.  For example, plants respond to light patterns generated by their owner's reading activity, and insects are drawn to patterns of a house that contain sweets.  In contrast to studies on organisms that respond to patterns, studies on neutral patterns that provoke an organism's reaction are scarce.  This study investigates the reaction of fruit flies to neutral patterns of light, sound, and smell.  The experiment's setup involves creating patterns of light, sound, and smell, and observing the response of fruit flies to these stimuli.  The reaction is measured by analyzing the movement of the flies within the test area.  The study discovers that all three types of patterns elicit a response from the flies, which is characterized as directed movement towards the source of the pattern.  Furthermore, the pattern's frequency, wavelength, and duration all impact the size of the response.  Interestingly, the response to these patterns is similar to that of a physical force, such as gravity, which pulls the flies towards their source regardless of their initial position.  This phenomenon is observed even when the flies are placed in the center of the test area, from which they fall towards the source of the pattern.  This behavior is observed even when the pattern is changed to a different shape, such as a circle, which the flies fall towards as well.  Additionally, the response to these patterns occurs even when the flies are placed in an area where they have previously experienced the pattern before, which suggests that the response is an immediate reaction to the pattern.  The study also analyzes the movement of the flies in more detail, which reveals that their movement follows a specific direction, which is referred to as coherence.  The study further finds that the level of coherence varies depending on the frequency of the pattern, with higher frequencies resulting in lower coherence.  The study also explores the possibility that the fly's response to these patterns may be an example of a broader phenomenon that could be observed in other organisms, which is referred to as pattern-induced motion.  The study provides empirical evidence for this phenomenon by demonstrating that the fly's response to these patterns is similar to that of other organisms that respond to patterns, such as plants that respond to light patterns.  The study further finds that the fly's brain processes the pattern in a specific way, which involves a particular type of cell that is sensitive to the pattern's frequency and wavelength.  The study presents a mathematical model that predicts the fly's response

This study introduces a novel character representation for representations of quantum groups, drawing from ideas in combinatorial algebra and geometry. Specifically, we define a character using combinatorial objects called cluster characters, and demonstrate that this character filters representations into distinct categories based on their combinatorial properties. Furthermore, we establish that both classical and Weyl group symmetries are naturally incorporated within this character framework. Additionally, we reveal that Iwama's formulas, previously derived through analytical methods, are inherently embedded within the structure of cluster characters. Moreover, we demonstrate that both classical and twisted representations of quantum groups exhibit similar behavior in this context. This study builds upon prior research by Nakanishi and Iwama, and presents a more comprehensive exploration of cluster characters as an organizing framework for representations of quantum groups. This work is a distillation of the author's Ph.D. thesis.

In our research, we tackle the challenge of learning in decentralized networks by addressing data disparities. We develop a new learning framework, DR-DSGD, which simultaneously minimizes the negative effects of distributional shifts and discrepancies between nodes. The DR-DSGD framework leverages over-represented neighbors to reduce the impact of data disparities and employs an adaptive per-node learning rate that responds to data disparities. We provide a rigorous analysis of the convergence rate of DR-DSGD and per-node learning rate updates. The optimal strategy for per-node learning rates per feature is per-weight. We conduct extensive experiments to validate the effectiveness of DR-DSGD against various types of data disparities. The results show that DR-DSGD achieves comparable or better performance when compared to centralized methods under similar communication constraints. The code for our research is publicly available on GitHub. DR-DSGD outperforms per-node per-iteration baselines, including D-PSGD, Fast-DIG, and FR-DIG, in our experiments. The analysis and experiments indicate that DR-DSGD converges at a rate of O(1/T) in the absence of data disparities, and its performance declines at a rate of O(1/√T) in the presence of moderate data disparities, and an experiment involving climate change classification demonstrates that DR-DSGD's performance decline is less pronounced with larger data disparities. The study of DR-DSGD provides valuable insights into the design of decentralized learning methods that are resistant to data disparities. Three new datasets are introduced as part of our contributions, namely Distri-Mnist, Distri-KDD, and Seasonal-CIFAR10, which pose significant challenges to existing decentralized learning methods. The evaluations of multiple methods on these new datasets highlight their disparities in robustness to data disparities. DR-DSGD emerges as one of the top-performing methods across all datasets in our research. The research offers practical recommendations for the selection of hyperparameters for DR-DSGD, and its scope is explored through theoretical extensions. Through a review of the contract's code and its evolution, we reveal its underlying components and reveal that it follows a traditional pyramid scheme model. As the scheme relies heavily on recruiting new members, it exhibits characteristics of a classic pyramid, with little to no legitimate business functionality. Analysis of the code's changes over time suggests that its creators made several adjustments to avoid detection by blockchain analysts, including modifying its investment returns and refund policies. We also investigate the Forsage network's social aspects, mapping its organizational hierarchy and identifying its key leaders. Through real-world transactions and user interactions, we validate the theoretical profitability of the scheme, demonstrating how participants can earn significant returns by recruiting new levels of the pyramid. Furthermore, we estimate the total value locked in the Forsage contract, as well as the circulating supply of the token used within the scheme. Our research also delves into the economic incentives provided by the scheme, including various rewards for users who refer new participants, as well as the penalties imposed on users who attempt to withdraw funds prematurely. We analyze the scheme's governance features, revealing how the code enforces critical rules and ensures the secure transfer of user funds. We discuss the legal ramifications of participating in such schemes and highlight the red flags exhibited by Forsage, as well as the challenges of detecting similar scams on blockchain platforms, especially those with advanced smart contract functionality. Finally, we explore the difficulties faced by law enforcement in tracking the transacting entities and the anonymous users within the Forsage network, underscoring the need for more effective and robust methods for analyzing blockchain data and identifying and disrupting cryptocurrency-based scams.
