Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized text game emulator that maintains compatibility with classic TextWorld levels and achieves an astonishing one million actions per second on a single CPU core.
When tested against a standard RL agent, TextWorldExpress demonstrates negligible differences in learning curves compared to traditional TextWorld environments.
The emulator's performance varies depending on level complexity, reaching as high as 460 kiloactions per second on a simple level and 160 kiloactions per second on a complex one.
TextWorldExpress boasts notable improvements over its predecessors, including significant reductions in memory usage and reliance on unnecessary system calls.
As a result, we discover that optimizing text games for better performance also translates to substantial gains in virtual machine speed. 
Ultimately, TextWorldExpress serves as an superior alternative to outdated text games, capable of supporting extensive training sessions in a single day on just a single GPU. 
The project's source code is available on GitHub under the MIT License, along with instructions on how to set up and use the emulator. 
Our research paper is freely accessible on arXiv, covering TextWorldExpress's development, performance assessments and benchmarking against contemporary text games. 
In recognition of TextWorldExpress's groundbreaking advancements, our research has been selected as the best paper submission for the 2020 TextWorld Competition. 
TextWorldExpress is compatible with both TextWorld and GVGAI, allowing it to support a wide range of text games spanning multiple themes, including fantasy, sports, adventure and more. 
The project's high-performance capabilities make it an ideal platform for conducting extensive virtual training sessions on both CPU and GPU cores. 
In a significant breakthrough, TextWorldExpress is shown to learn complex game strategies at a rate more than 3 times faster than traditional text games. 
The project's high-performance virtual machine is also found to fix a long-standing issue with reinforcement learning algorithms, where artificial fluctuations in performance are eliminated, resulting in more stable learning curves. 
In recognition of its groundbreaking performance, TextWorldExpress is proposed as a standard for high-performance text games, along with a new benchmark called TextWorldExpress Lite, along with three other competition-level games. 
The research paper is subsequently selected as one of the cover stories for the journal

Our findings, based on an experimental and theoretical analysis, suggest that models perform best when the restricted data set includes relevant information and is free from both noisy and misleading information. Notably, the performance boost from data restriction is particularly noticeable in low-data settings. Our study's results also provide insight into the types of regularization that data restriction affords, indicating it acts as both a form of label regularization and noise reduction. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the efficacy of data restriction on enhancing the performance of multiple NLP models across different tasks. By exploring the theoretical aspects of data restriction, our study highlights the role of information density in influencing model performance. Finally, our work shows that data restriction can be an effective yet straightforward method to incorporate additional forms of regularization in model training. Overall, our study's findings can facilitate a deeper understanding of the effects of data restriction and label regularization on NLP models, while also highlighting the practical benefits of this technique for enhancing model performance. Additionally, our research raises several theoretical questions regarding the effects of data restriction, along with potential methodologies for experimentally testing the approach's generalizability. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive examination of the principles and practices underlying data restriction, with implications for both our theoretical understanding and future experimental design. Ultimately, our research underscores the value of a pragmatic approach, emphasizing the importance of experimentally verifying theoretical hypotheses through repeated testing. In quantum field theories, the concept of charge convexity plays a significant role in ensuring that physical observables remain well-defined. A crucial aspect is the requirement that charged states comply with the principle of convexity, which can be violated if a state transforms into multiple distinct states upon traveling through spatial distances. Recently, a study revealed that primary fields maintain charge convexity in conformal field theories, which is a fundamental aspect of the Feeble Gravity Conjecture. However, this study discovered that secondary field operators can lose convexity property. These findings provide a deeper insight into the relationship between charge convexity and the representation of field operators in conformal field theories. Although they do not offer a solution to the Feeble Gravity Conjecture, they shed light on a possible direction to address it. The possible connection between charge convexity and the Holographic Conjecture is also discussed. A distinct feature of this study is the use of free field theories as a reference point for evaluating secondary field operators, which is a common practice in studies related to the Feeble Gravity Conjecture. Another key aspect of this study is the use of transformation properties under the conformal group to investigate charge convexity, which differentiates it from previous research related to this topic. A new inequality derived from the Feichtinger's inequality plays a crucial role in demonstrating that primary field operators maintain charge convexity. Furthermore, this study explores how secondary field operators can acquire non-convex structure through recombination of primary field operators, which provides a clear, concise, and intuitive explanation of this phenomenon. The paper is organized in the following manner: an introduction to charge convexity, recombination of field operators, and the Feeble Gravity Conjecture sets the stage, a review of existing literature on this topic follows, and then a new inequality is introduced along with a detailed explanation of its derivation. The study then delves into the specific case of free field theories, which includes a discussion on the choice of reference point, the use of transformation properties under the conformal group, and a demonstration of non-convex structure in secondary field operators. The paper concludes with a discussion on its findings and a review of its content. A detailed explanation of the used notation and a comprehensive bibliography complete the study. The main contributions of this study are a new inequality, a demonstration of non-convex structure in secondary field operators, and a clear, concise, and intuitive explanation of this phenomenon. The new model retains the core features of the original ASPM, incorporating elements from the Generalised Bertrand Model and the Double Auction Model to explore how firms' strategic behavior affects their own wholesale prices and revenue. Our model offers procedural guidelines for determining optimal procurement prices and revenue guarantees, taking into account firms' willingness to engage in wholesale market activity. We experimentally evaluate the models using simulated data, finding that the new ASPM model yields the most realistic firm behavior and revenue outcomes. Ultimately, our findings suggest that Australian wholesale electricity market policy developers should consider a more comprehensive procurement model that accounts for market engagement. The proposed model provides a framework for exploring how firms' behavior in the wholesale market influence their own pricing and revenue, which could also be applied to other critical services subject to procurement. We are defining a new convex cone, comprised of square matrices whose smallest eigenvalue is positive. This cone, denoted as $\Delta_n$, shares many properties with the convex cone of positive semidefinite matrices, $\Sigma_n$, as they both possess analogous elements and can be represented using similar matrix representations. However, unlike $\Sigma_n$, the dual of $\Delta_n$ is notomorphic to $\Sigma_n$. A key function related to $\Delta_n$, $x\mapsto x^T K x$, is not an even function when the matrix $K$ is an element of $\Delta_n$. This property gives rise to an interesting inequality demonstrating that the absolute value of a matrix $K$ within $\Delta_n$ is not equal to the same matrix, but rather results in a matrix within $\Sigma_n$. These characteristics provide a foundation for investigating the potential applications of $\Delta_n$ across optimization and systems and control theory. A discussion on existing literature and potential future research paths is also initiated within this study. Furthermore, we outline an efficient conversion process for any convex optimization problem set within $\Delta_n$ to be transformed into an equivalent problem within $\Sigma_n$, as well as presenting an initial example of an optimization problem defined using $\Delta_n$. This problem example illustrates an instance where the proposed conversion method yields a significantly more efficient optimal solution than previously reported. Lastly, we also present an alternative representation for any element $K$ within $\Delta_n$, expressed in terms of its block diagonal and skew-block diagonal components, which collectively provide a more comprehensive exploration of the properties and potential applications of the $\Delta_n$ cone. Ultimately, this research aims to provide a thorough examination of the convex cone $\Delta_n$ and its numerous connections to existing literature, as well as to introduce an initial framework for investigating its role across optimization and systems and control theory. Concurrent visual and inertial measurements from a system's internal sensors enable navigation within complex environments. Nonetheless, estimating a system's translation, rotation, and other entities' positions relies heavily on external memory regarding the environment's characteristics, which can significantly impact estimation accuracy. Current approaches to visual-inertial navigation neglect the impact of environmental factors on estimation, failing to account for phenomena such as light reflection, shadows, and water reflections that affect camera observations and inertial measurements. To address these challenges, a novel external memory attention mechanism is proposed, allowing a system to prioritize relevant internal and external information when estimating its position and orientation. This proposed mechanism is integrated with an optimization-based visual-inertial odometry framework to enhance estimation performance, particularly in scenarios with low-resolution images, extended periods of airtime, and varied environmental reflections, as demonstrated in simulation and real-world testing. Experimental results show that the proposed method yields better translation and rotation estimation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art baseline methods. Additionally, sequential action selection strategy is also explored to demonstrate the potential of action-aware visual-inertial navigation in complex scenarios with varied environmental reflections, shadows, and objects, as shown in additional real-world experiments. Code for the paper is publicly available at https://github.com/PRVIOLab/EMA-VIO.. This research is an extension of an earlier work presented at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2020.  Further, a video illustrating the method's performance in comparison to baseline methods can be found at https://youtu.be/6c1b3D3D3fQ.  In contrast to previous visual-inertial navigation methods that rely on the system's intrinsic sensors, the proposed method's estimation accuracy is significantly enhanced by leveraging the system's external memory regarding its surroundings, as shown in a series of challenging scenarios. This achievement is an significant breakthrough in the field of visual-inertial navigation, enabling the estimation of a system's position, orientation, and other entities' positions within complex environments that have varied reflections, shadows, and objects, as demonstrated in real-world testing. This finding has important implications for the development of advanced visual-inertial navigation systems that can operate effectively in a wide range of environments, and its impact will be analyzed in the discussion section. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation gradually slows down.  By incorporating various tidal interactions with planets and the stellar interior, we develop a set of equations describing how a star's rotation rate changes over time.  Considering how these tidal interactions affect the star's interior and outer layers is crucial in understanding its overall behavior.  Building on previous work by Irwin (2014), we update the prescription for how the star's differential rotation changes.  Specifically, we account for instances where the outer layers may rotate opposite to the interior.  This could occur in stars that have undergone significant contraction.  Integrating these updates into our equations, we simulate solar-type stars undergoing magnetic field generation and rotation evolution.  Our simulations reveal that anti-solar differential rotation can lead to a stronger toroidal magnetic field, eventually driven by the star's decreasing rotation rate.  However, this increase is limited by the development of magnetic instabilities.  The strength of this field component may reach several megagauss before the star's magnetic cycle disappears due to its low rotation rate.  The formation of magnetic islands within the star's convection zone enhances the generation of poloidal magnetic field, potentially creating cyclic patterns.  This cyclic field generation may emerge in stars with rotation rates as low as 0.434 times the present solar rotation rate.  The time scales for these cycles vary from 11 to 75 days, corresponding to the star's rotation period.  The duration of these cycles is expected to prolong as the star continues to age.  This predicts the existence of magnetic cycles in gradually rotating stars that are about 0.5 billion years old and older.  The detection of these cycles in stars with slow rotation rates, particularly in the Kepler data, should be re-examined with enhanced signal processing techniques.  The generation of magnetic cycles in these stars may also result in coronal activity, affecting their stellar evolution and surrounding planetary environments.  The emergence of magnetic cycles in these stars may also have implications for the formation and maintenance of planetary magnetic fields.  Furthermore, this process may contribute to the generation of magnetic fields in stars that are born without a parental external magnetic field.  This scenario may provide a possible explanation for the presence of magnetic fields in newborn stars that are born through molecular cloud collapse.  The generation of magnetic cycles in these stars may also set a minimum strength for the magnetic field in stars, regardless of their birth history.  This minimum field strength, coupled with the star's mass and internal structure, may influence its evolution

Our research indicates that the number of 2-torsion points on an elliptic curve, denoted by $\tau$, influences its rank. Specifically, as $\tau$ increases, the rank of the elliptic curve also increases. We establish criteria for curves to have higher ranks based on properties of their $j$-invariants and 2-torsion configurations. Moreover, under the assumption that curves with specific $j$-invariant values and 2-torsion configurations are dense, we can determine the distribution of ranks according to $\tau$. Our findings contribute to our broader research aiming to understand rank distribution within quartic extensions. Recent breakthroughs in numerical computation, driven by GPU and TPU advancements, have significantly sped up various quantum many-body algorithms, essentially making them 'efficient'. This study uncovers the underlying reason for this improvement by demonstrating that most modern algorithm implementations, specifically involving tensor network methods including GPU-driven GPU-TN and TPU-driven TTN, approximate the solution using a simple trick - by decomposing the matrix product state into a minimal quantum circuit consisting of only single-qubit gates and nearest-neighbor two-qubit gates. In order to evaluate the computational accuracy of this circuit approximation, we developed an exact online carrier for circuit matrix products, leveraging the decomposition property. Furthermore, we explore the entanglement properties associated with such circuit states and show that they are closely related to the original matrix states. Lastly, we discuss potential applications of this research in both scientific domains, highlighting potential improvements to tensor network algorithms as well as potential breakthroughs in quantum computing, notably in the demonstration of quantum computational supremacy in near-term, fault-tolerant devices. The success of cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcomes depends heavily on the properties of cancer tissues that are spatially embedded, as stated in the spatial cancer biology paradigm.  Despite the wealth of information that can be obtained from digital slides, many cancer-related genomic alterations remain unexplained.  A recent study combining cancer genomics and spatial transcriptomics finds that a large portion of the cancer genome is comprised of functional regions that control cell density within tumors.  However, a comprehensive understanding of the underlying tumor topology and the organization of the cancer cell landscape remains elusive.  Cancer networks, constructed from tissue samples using mutual k-nearest neighbors, exhibit a hierarchical structure with varying resolution that can be leveraged for analysis.  By applying hierarchical techniques such as graph mini-topsdoms and hierarchical graph embeddings, these networks can be efficiently processed and their intricate structure better captured.  Our research employs a graph mini-topdom approach to build a hierarchical cancer network and pinpoints specific topological characteristics that differentiate normal and tumor cells.  Normal cells are more likely to reside at the surface of the graph, while tumor cells are found at various depths.  A subsequent hierarchical graph embedding revealed that certain features hold importance at every level of the graph, while others are only crucial in specific mini-topdoms.  Our methodology can be used to identify cell populations based on their location within the graph and the surrounding topology.  By building a hierarchical cancer network using multiple tissue samples, we can perform multi-graph mini-topdom analysis and uncover that different tissues share similar low-level graph topological characteristics but have unique middle and high-level structures.  Furthermore, our research can be used to create novel, topology-aware cancer markers that pinpoint the location of specific cell populations within the tumor tissue and provide a new perspective on the long-standing epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition hypothesis. Point processes that take into account the self and inter-activations of events are widely used in networks to model occurrence patterns of phenomena such as neural activity, stock market fluctuations, and earthquake epicenter development.  A primary point process model that accounts for both types of connections is the nonlinear Hawkes process, and we have developed a Bayesian approach to estimating its parameters.  By utilizing the noncentered Bayesian formulation, our method tackles the challenges typically associated with nonlinear models, such as nonidentifiability and non-Gaussian error distributions.  We demonstrate through simulated data that our approach effectively recovers parameter values, and in networks observed in reality, such as neural network data and earthquake data, our method shows a superior performance when compared to standard Bayesian estimation, particularly in cases of non-Gaussian data.  Furthermore, we investigate various aspects of our approach, including the consequences of nonidentifiability, and provide a user-friendly guide for implementing our method. Overall, our study offers a thorough examination of the nonlinear Hawkes process, including its challenges, our method, and potential extensions, such as the inclusion of exogenous influences, latent variables, and state-space models. Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable performance in medical image segmentation, the process is often hindered by a lack of well-labeled training data. Semi-supervised learning offers a potential solution by leveraging a small labeled dataset and a large unlabelled dataset to improve network performance. We propose a contrastive semi-supervised learning method to conduct cross-annotation segmentation on similar anatomical structures by exploring the underlying similarities between annotations. By pre-training a starting network on a large unlabelled dataset with a super-resolution task, we leverage the underlying patterns in images. We then employ a semi-supervised learning technique to update the network using a labeled dataset with annotations in question, and refine the network to recognize patterns that distinguish it from irrelevant annotations through contrastive loss functions. The network is then adapted to perform segmentation tasks on unseen annotations by leveraging domain adaptation techniques. Experimental results on segmenting two comparable anatomical structures, the aortic arch and descending aorta, in chest CT scans, demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing semi-supervised learning approaches. Furthermore, we showcase the efficacy of our method by applying it to cross-annotation segmentation between the left atrium and right atrium in chest CT scans. The method's effectiveness is illustrated with a demonstration video available at: https://youtu.be/kt1DwQDqG9Y. Additionally, we highlight potential challenges and avenues for research in the field. The 1.5 order formulation of supersymmetric theories has been analyzed for its underlying structure. Contrary to its intended goal, the study reveals that employing 1.5 order transformations instead of full order ones leads to an inconsistent algebra and yields a nilpotent ghost operator with an order of $s^2=\Delta$. This finding challenges the proposed concept of a nilpotent operator of order $s^2=1$ as a prerequisite for the BRST formalism. The study maintains that the 1.5 order framework is an unrefined representation of the BRST algebra and suggests modifying the nilpotent operator to $s^2=D$ for a legitimate 1.4 order transformation. The research also identifies the spurious volume factor issue characteristic of 1.5 order theories. It's shown that only one type of operator maintains coherent rotation properties, aligning with previous findings in the half-space setup. We also explore rotating AdS$_2$ shells and their connections to boundary points in AdS$_3$. Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however they will likely be contaminated by delensing noise. To improve their sensitivity, it is essential to estimate delensing biases accurately. By using a machine learning technique to predict lensing maps from microwave data, our research demonstrates that the predicted maps can be utilized to regulate the delensing bias, thereby reducing the estimated bias by a factor of three. Additionally, our research explores the feasibility of applying this approach in the presence of primordial tensor fluctuations. By employing a neural network to forecast lensing maps, we investigate various factors that influence the performance of this approach, including the amount of training data, training techniques, and neural network architecture. Our findings suggest that a well-trained neural network can effectively estimate the delensing bias, reducing the estimated bias by a factor of five. However, in scenarios where primordial tensor fluctuations are significant, the performance of the neural network is impaired by the presence of signal loss due to delensing, leading to an increased scatter in estimated biases. By examining future experimental designs, we find that even in the most challenging scenarios, a well-trained neural network is able to estimate the delensing bias with a precision of $\sigma(r)/r \approx 0.01$ in one dimension, and by combining this approach with four-component vector delensing, the estimation precision can be as high as $\sigma(r)/r \approx 0.001$. Therefore, incorporating this method into future experiments will significantly improve their ability to measure the $r$ parameter. By doing so, the estimated value of $r$ will be more accurate and reliable, especially in scenarios where primordial tensor fluctuations are prominent. This research provides a new avenue for exploring the delensing of microwave background maps, and the results obtained are applicable to a wide range of future experimental designs. By utilizing this approach in conjunction with semi-analytical estimators, future experiments will be able to measure the $r$ parameter with even greater precision, potentially as low as $0.01$ in the most challenging scenarios. This research is relevant to a range of future experiments, including the Simulated CMB Experiment, CMB-S4, and BICEP/Keck Program, and the results obtained are expected to significantly improve the measurement precision of the $r$ parameter in these experiments. This research is an important step towards the optimal use of machine learning in the analysis of microwave background maps, and the results obtained will be relevant in the near future

We establish a new concept, 'partial uniform ellipticity' on a specific domain, and prove it's equivalent to a modified version of the stage set condition from [CS17]. This equivalence enables us to leverage results related to partial uniform ellipticity to demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions for second-order elliptic and parabolic equations within the stage set framework. Additionally, we show that standard weakly continuous operators satisfy the stage set condition, and we provide a new proof for the existence and uniqueness of solutions for monotone operators under the stage set condition. These results build upon prior work while particularly considering the case when the stage set condition is not necessarily full-dimensional. 

We then explore potential improvements to our findings and related questions. Firstly, we investigate whether strong solutions can be obtained from weak solutions in cases where partial uniform ellipticity is present. Secondly, we aim to extend our results to higher-order operators while assuming the stage set condition. Lastly, we examine whether coercivity can be derived from the stage set condition for operators that are not necessarily monotone. 

On top of that, we apply our findings to a specific problem, namely a nonhomogeneous mean curvature flow with surface tension, and demonstrate that it can be reformulated as a family of second-order elliptic equations under the stage set condition. This, in turn, yields existence and uniqueness results for this specific problem. 

Finally, we discuss potential connections between our results and prior work, especially in relation to the stage set condition and partial uniform ellipticity, while also exploring new directions and questions that arise from our findings.

By building upon a pre-trained language model and utilizing a sparse token representation to identify feature patterns, our network can efficiently identify social factors in health contexts. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by training and evaluating the model on a comprehensive dataset covering 139 diverse social factors, with outstanding performance and exceptional generalization capabilities on previously unseen data. Furthermore, we showcase the model's potential to streamline the labeling process for a smaller subset of data, thereby expanding its applicability to a wide range of machine learning tasks involving text data. To address health concerns related to 5G technology, a detailed analysis of 5G mast emissions was conducted to provide quantitative data on the exposure children receive when attending school or spending time in medical facilities. Statistical models were used to gather relevant information on 5G mast locations, children's exposure, and cellular network characteristics across the UK, Ireland, Netherlands, Belgium, and Switzerland. However, the study's primary focus was on UK data. According to the findings, the exposure children receive from 5G masts is significantly lower than their exposure from cell phones. In fact, the analysis shows that, on average, 4G exposure exceeds 5G exposure by a factor of 50,000, while the ratio of child-to-adult 4G exposure is approximately 1.5, indicating children may already be receiving higher 4G exposures at home and in schools than recommended limits. A comparison of these figures to the average exposure from 5G masts, 0.00056 volts, shows that children receive about 25 times the in-building 5G exposure from masts than from within their own homes. To minimize this exposure, researchers suggest locating 5G masts farther away from schools and medical facilities, in accordance with international guidelines, or considering the deployment of smaller, lower-power 5G cells. This paper compares the efficiency of two reduced basis method variations - 
a) a unified approach and 
b) a segmented approach - 
in addressing Fluid-Structure Interactions (FSIs) problems.
The two techniques differ in how they handle the diverse nature of 
linear/nonlinear fluid and solid equations.
The unified approach treats all equations equally, 
while the segmented approach tailors a specific offline/online strategy 
to the fluid and solid problems being considered.
To evaluate these methods, a sample Fluid-Structure Interaction problem 
from cardiovascular dynamics was used, with both a compressible and incompressible flow model for the fluid component.
The results show that the choice of strategy depends on the specific 
problem being solved, with the unified approach being more adaptable. 
However, for problems with similar dimensionality (such as two-dimensional solid and fluid components), 
the segmented approach yields better performance. 
Furthermore, it was observed that the majority of computational time is spent 
on the expensive evaluation of the residual, with a potential for further efficiency gains. 
As a result, further research into more efficient algorithms for the segregated approach is recommended. 
On the other hand, with an anticipated move towards higher-order and more complex models in the next generation of cardiovascular simulations, 
the ability of the unified approach to adapt to these changes makes it particularly suitable for such applications. 
Therefore, both the unified and the segmented approach continue to be relevant and deserving of further investigation. 
As such, a further numerical test has been set out in the concluding section to explore their performance in solving more demanding FSI problems. 
Here, a condition of flow turbulence has been introduced into the sample problem from cardiovascular dynamics, 
along with a discussion on the impending modifications that will be necessary to handle the more complicated simulations of the next generation seamlessly. 
The modifications in question pertain to the introduction of turbulent flow models, the use of non-dimensionalized coordinates, 
and the incorporation of more sophisticated fluid dynamics, such as multiphase and Navier-Stokes equations, 
as well as the expected move to more advanced solvers, more powerful computers, and more efficient algorithms. 
With these advancements in mind, it is essential to revisit and revise the existing reduced basis approach solutions, 
especially in the healthcare field, to ensure a smooth path for the next generation of computational researchers.

For agents to effectively navigate unfamiliar environments, having an efficient navigation system is crucial. Topological maps have shown significant promise in this area by allowing agents to navigate using abstract representations of spaces, facilitating easy path planning and localization. However, traditional approaches to creating topological maps face several challenges, including the need for extensive exploration data and the ability to accurately identify topological features. This paper introduces HiTMap, a novel hierarchical topological map representation that leverages light detection and ranging (LiDAR) data to create a hierarchical diagram of the environment. This representation utilizes a non-overlapping grid structure to organize navigation metrics, including proximity, obstacle avoidance, and energy efficiency. We demonstrate the efficacy of HiTMap by applying it to the navigation of a complex indoor space, showcasing that it yields optimal paths that are at least 20% more energy-efficient compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, HiTMap exhibits 10% higher localization accuracy than a state-of-the-art approach, while requiring significantly less training data. These advancements make HiTMap an attractive solution for creating robust and adaptable navigation systems. This research is an extension of our previous work presented at IROS 2022. This paper provides a more in-depth analysis of the representation, along with a more comprehensive discussion of state-of-the-art topological maps and our unique contributions. We have also included a more detailed explanation of the HiTMap architecture and a clearer description of the evaluation methodology. These updates highlight the benefits of using a hierarchical structure, along with a more thorough examination of the performance of the system. As parallel programs are becoming more complex to solve real-world problems, the need for efficient and scalable memory management has increased across various computing platforms, including GPUs.  Despite its potential, object-based programming on GPUs has been hinderedly by the lack of a suitable memory management system.  This research presents DynaSOAr, a novel concurrent memory allocator that leverages single-occupancy arrays to facilitate object-based programming on GPUs with optimized memory access.  By combining time-space tradeoff optimization and address generation techniques, DynaSOAr provides a high-performance memory management system that accelerates memory-intensive memory access.  This is further enhanced by a dynamic size configuration that optimizes memory utilization and reduces memory waste.  Our experiments demonstrate that DynaSOAr achieves significant performance improvements, up to 3 times faster than existing memory allocators, for a range of object-based applications on different GPUs.  This research provides a foundation for the development of efficient and flexible memory management systems that can tackle memory-intensive challenges on GPUs.  This is particularly relevant as the growing interest in heterogeneous programming requires a memory management system that can effectively utilize the unique characteristics of CPUs, GPUs, and other computing cores. Recently, implicit neural architectures have generated significant interest for creating multi-output functions, such as 3D point clouds, graphs, and maps, with impressive results. However, implementing instance segmentation using implicit functions is complicated due to their inherent simplicity, representing all instances as separate implicit functions. To overcome this challenge, we introduce FourierMask, a novel instance segmentation framework that utilizes Fourier mapping to divide the unit interval into distinct regions for each instance, enabling the implicit representation to capture multiple objects within a single function. Through Fourier analysis, we derive a derivative-based loss function that enhances separation and cohesion, leverages Fourier coefficients to promote coherence, and prevents region overlap by analyzing interval divisions. FourierMask achieves notable improvements in instance segmentation accuracy on the MINC-255K dataset and real-world applications, such as animal detection and medical organ segmentation, particularly when compared to recent implicit architectures and methods. Moreover, FourierMask demonstrates adaptability when integrated with other implicit functions, demonstrating its versatility and effectiveness. Code is available at https://github.com/lygxt/FourierMask.

The vast majority of existing music search engines rely on keyword-based approaches, which can lead to unappealing results if the desired music is not correctly identified by these methods. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel music search concept, centered around a meta-query that encompasses multiple song characteristics. This framework allows users to express their search intentions with a degree of abstraction, effectively allowing for a level of imperfection in results. We showcase a practical application of this idea by developing a search engine that combines a proprietary character recognition system with a robust matching mechanism to deliver a practical solution for searching music by humming. Our experimental findings highlight the advantages of our approach over traditional keyword-based search engines. We also explore the extension of this model to accommodate additional query types, such as lyrics and melody-only searches, ultimately demonstrating the potential for our approach to become a unified music search platform. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub under the MIT License. Moreover, we have launched a web interface for our music search engine at https://music.ismir2023.org/. This engine allows users to search for songs by humming or singing into their browser. It is also possible to access our engine through the CMU Mobile App available on Google Play and Apple Store. This app enables users to search for songs anywhere, anytime. It is worth noting that our engine is constantly being updated with more training data, particularly in the form of wider melody bases and richer semantic annotations. In recognition of the significant advancements in music search technology, the ISMIR 2023 conference has chosen our paper as one of the outstanding contributions, worthy of an additional presentation in the form of a video. This video provides a comprehensive overview of our research through an engaging narrative. It has received over 10,000 views on YouTube. Our innovative music search approach has inspired the creation of several follow-up projects, such as the development of a music search interface for the HNSK database, as well as initiatives to promote music search technology through challenges and competitions. Our work has also been featured in an interview with the KTN podcast, covering our research and its broader implications. In addition, we have been awarded the Best Demo Paper Award at the 31st ACM International Conference on Multimedia for our music search engine demo. This award recognizes the exceptional interactivity and engaging nature of our demonstration, providing an immersive experience for conference attendees. We have also been invited to present our research at the prestigious Google Research Seminar Series. Godel's onetenth rule has been introduced in 1932 by Emil Godel to eliminate circular arguments in intuitionism. Over time, researchers discovered that this rule can be expressed through modal equivalence formulas, specifically using the box-necessity operator 'Bp' to capture its essential reasoning properties. This rule has become crucial in providing soundness proofs for various separation and completion methods in constraint solving. However, Godel's rule is known to be incomplete for modal logic when using only the standard semantics. To address this issue, researchers introduced the concept of preimage semantics, which makes the rule complete and highly desirable for its intuitive simplicity. This paper builds upon preimage semantics by introducing the concept of preimage structures and preimage modal logics. We demonstrate that logics based on preimage structures can emulate the reasoning of (i) classical modal logic with preimage semantics, (ii) hybrid logic with modal correspondence relations, and (iii) fuzzy modal logic with operators for (ii 1/2 p,q)-meets and (ii 1/2 p,q)-joins. Furthermore, we explore the expressiveness of preimage structures and demonstrate that they can represent (i) circularity conditions for modal logic with preimage semantics, (ii) hybrid logic with modal correspondence relations, and (iii) fuzzy modal logic with (ii 1/2 p,q)-meets and (ii 1/2 p,q)-joins. We also examine the relationship between preimage structures and modal logics based on the Godel operator, and investigate whether they can capture the reasoning of modal logic with preimage semantics, hybrid logic with modal correspondence relations, and fuzzy modal logic with (ii 1/2 p,q)-meets and (ii 1/2 p,q)-joins. The Hele-Shaw cell, a semi-confined medium with a thin layer of high-viscosity fluid, has been extensively studied for its striking interplay of surface tension and viscous forces. Research has revealed the unique properties of finger growth in this setup, which is influenced by both disorder and external fields. This paper delves into the previously unexplored realm of the Hele-Shaw cell that is rotating rapidly. As the inner fluid is displaced from the center, an inward flow develops, producing an asymmetrical pressure gradient that pushes fingers apart. This pressure effect overpowers the confining layer's viscosity, dictating the behavior of the spreading fingers. This dominance allows the creation of highly irregular patterns by adjusting the cell's rotation speed. This discovery holds significant implications for our understanding of the Hele-Shaw cell, highlighting the versatility of this model in exhibiting a wide range of patterns due to the flexibility of its governing equations. This finding is further validated by numerical simulations, which accurately replicate the observed phenomena. This research provides a theoretical framework for analyzing the rotating Hele-Shaw cell, and it is anticipated that this model will contribute to the better understanding of viscous flow in complex systems such as volcanic landscapes and oil reservoirs. This study also offers a scope for further exploration into the behavior of this cell when external fields are manipulated. This could potentially enable the development of a new class of mixed-convection systems that are self-sustaining and could be applied in various applications such as oil extraction and environmental monitoring. This work is a result of a collaborative effort between experimental and theoretical researchers, and it paves the way for further interdisciplinary research in this area. Ethynyl cyclopentadiene exists in two isomeric forms, and we outline their structural characteristics. This process involves two phases: initial assessment by Tezos nodes and later verification of contracts through a commander-in-chief node. Our research focuses on enhancing the second verification phase by introducing a novel validation tool, HELMHOLTZ, tailored for Tezos smart contracts expressed in Michelson using Quotient Types and Refinement Types. By leveraging the refinement types, developers can mark valid Michelson expressions, thereby allowing HELMHOLTZ to efficiently identify genuine refinements from suspected ones with a type-checking time of approximately 10 microseconds on average. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of HELMHOLTZ by applying our method to a notable smart contract and comparing its performance with the existing Tezos implementation. Furthermore, we explore potential security benefits and a notable reduction in assessment time by incorporating Refinement Types, an area we plan to explore further in upcoming research. This research was initially presented at the TAPAS 2020 Workshop. HELMHOLTZ has been successfully integrated into the Tezo's testing environment, TestKit, and is presently being developed for the Bichon and Alba compilers. We explore the concept of Ramsey character in Boolean posets that have a V-shape, examining how the Ramsey character behaves for these posets as we vary the size of the ground set. Notably, we establish a connection between the Ramsey character and another property called the 'weakly Ramsey' property, also depending on the poset's depth and the number of elements. Furthermore, we establish an upper limit for the Ramsey character when the ground set's cardinality is relatively large in comparison to the number of elements within the poset. Additionally, we provide a general formula for the Ramsey character when the ground set's cardinality is equal to the number of elements within the poset, and this formula is expressed through the poset's depth and its number of elements. Alongside this, we establish a lower bound for the Ramsey character, indicating that this lower bound matches the upper bound we established in cases where the ground set's cardinality is twice the number of elements within the poset. It's worth noting that previous research by Loiseau and Vigneron-Tomayo on V-shaped posets has provided a general lower bound for the Ramsey character, although this previous study placed no restrictions on the structure of these posets. Finally, we broaden the study to Boolean structures that have a V-shape by defining a specific ordering, referred to as the 'Boolean order', and subsequently determining the Ramsey character for this order when the ground set's cardinality is double the number of elements within the poset, revealing that the Ramsey character is directly equal to this double count in such cases. Ultimately, this order is shown to be highly analogous to the original V-shaped order, thereby allowing us to derive comparable yet distinct Ramsey character values. Additionally, we establish that the 'weakly Ramsey' property for Boolean structures that have a V-shape always implies the presence of a specific order, referred to as the 'anti-Boolean order', which in turn indicates that the Ramsey character will be greater than the number of elements within the poset, although this condition may not be necessary. Lastly, we explore various generalizations of both the original V-shaped order and the Boolean order by introducing distinct order definitions for different subsets within the structure, and by establishing that the 'weakly Ramsey' property for structures of this nature always implies the presence of one of these ordered definitions. Furthermore, this implies that the Ramsey character for such structures will always be greater than the number of elements within the poset, thereby providing a universal lower bound for all such structures.

In the context of information retrieval, where we deal with a dataset of $n$ multidimensional points, we aim to label each point as either 'clustered' or'single'. This is based on an unknown function $f$, which designates a specific cluster for each point unless it falls outside a distance of $\alpha$ from any cluster center. Our primary goal is to identify points likely to be single by examining their surroundings, thereby reducing unnecessary computation within clusters. To accomplish this, we develop a pyramidal approach to determine which points are likely isolated, thereby achieving a significant reduction in the overall computational time. For the remaining points marked as 'clustered', we employ a ball-tree data structure to further refine our assessment of which points are single. As a result, our algorithm yields an approximate solution to the dynamic $k$-means clustering problem with a lower time complexity of $O(n \log n)$, compared to $O(n^2)$, allowing us to handle larger datasets with ease. Furthermore, we prove the optimality of our solution by demonstrating a lower bound of $n \log n$ for this problem. Moreover, we showcase the effectiveness of our algorithm through extensive experiments on diverse datasets. Notably, we can tackle real-world high-dimensional text datasets with up to $50,000$ points and $200$ dimensions. Our approach also facilitates a near-optimal solution for a variant of the dynamic $k$-means clustering problem. Additionally, we explore connections to other clustering problems, such as dynamic $k$-center and dynamic facility location. Lastly, we discuss open questions and potential avenues for further research. As the underlying function $f$ is unknown, we develop our algorithm and analysis within a general framework, making our approach applicable across multiple scenarios. Furthermore, we examine specific instantiations of our framework, thereby obtaining insights into how our general approach yields optimal solutions for certain configurations. As a result, our research contributes to a broader understanding of dynamic clustering problems and provides opportunities for further exploration within the field. Ultimately, our work highlights the intricacies and challenges inherent to solving high-dimensional clustering problems, particularly those with unknown underlying structures. As such, we believe our results will yield valuable insights for future research endeavors. As we delve into the world of high-dimensional clustering, it becomes evident that multiple dimensions can pose significant computational challenges, thereby emphasizing the importance of exploring alternative approaches that leverage dimensionality reduction techniques, such as PCA, in further research. In the context of statistical inference, a nontransitive likelihood occurs when there's an unordered trio of parameters, say A, B, and C, for which the sampling probability is higher for sampling A than B, C for sampling B than C, and C for sampling C than A, holding true under specific conditions. We demonstrate that this phenomenon can happen even in the absence of circular reasoning. Furthermore, we show that circular relationships can lead to nontransitive likelihoods and present a comprehensive classification of these circumstances. Lastly, we explore the implications of nontransitive likelihoods on standard statistical procedures. Additionally, we discuss potential applications in designing data efficient sampling strategies. Finally, we conclude by outlining open research questions related to nontransitive likelihoods. We append supplementary material containing additional details on our results. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly in suppressing noise, and CycleGAN-based methods have emerged as a promising approach. These methods utilize unconstrained high-dose CT images as noise-free references to train noise addition cycles and adversarial networks to mimic the image transformation process. However, the existing cycle-based architectures have limitations, including the assumption that low-dose and high-dose CT images are directly connected, which overlooks the complex CT imaging process, including Poisson noise, photon counting, and log-intensity transformations. To address these challenges, we developed an adaptive inception layer-based switchable CycleGAN, incorporating adaptive inception layers and a switchable architecture, to effectively extract CT-specific features and learn the complex transformations between low-dose and high-dose CT images. Moreover, we integrated a noise injection module to simulate counting photon noise in low-dose CT images, thereby obtaining a more realistic noise-statistical consistency between the input and reconstructed images. When evaluated on a public lung CT dataset, our method demonstrated superior noise reduction performance, compared to cycle-based and non-cycle-based state-of-the-art methods, in both subjective visual assessment and objective metric evaluation. Moreover, our method successfully preserved important image details and edges, resulting in a more natural and less noisy image enhancement. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method outperforms existing cycle-based and non-cycle-based methods in terms of both quantitative and qualitative performance. When applied to actual low-dose CT datasets from clinical settings, our method effectively suppressed noise while preserving edge and texture, resulting in enhanced image quality. For dialog comprehension, numerous challenges arise due to the free-form nature of dialog conversations, which are often unstructured and unorganized. Current approaches to dialog comprehension often rely on strong contextual representations, which can be achieved via pre-trained models on large datasets. However, such datasets are typically mixed with other data types, such as solvers and knowledge bases, which can complicate the training process and result in contextual representations that are overly specialized. To address this issue, this research introduces a semi-supervised pre-trained model called SPACE-2, which utilizes a small set of labeled data to distinguish between dialog conversations and other types of text during a tree-structured pre-training process. This approach helps to prevent the model from developing a narrow focus on dialog conversations and allows it to leverage a diverse range of unlabelled data, which includes dialog pairs, dialog-solver pairs, and dialog-annotation pairs. When evaluated on the Dialog-State-Tracking task, our approach outperforms strong baselines, which include multi-task learning and adversarial training. Additionally, our approach demonstrates substantial performance gains on smaller datasets, which is critical for various low-resource dialog datasets. Furthermore, our approach surpasses the existing state-of-the-art on the Dialog-State-Tracking task when evaluated on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset. Our proposed method also demonstrates comparable performance to other state-of-the-art methods while being computationally efficient, making it an attractive solution for real-world video SR applications. We also release a comprehensive benchmark, named VSR Benchmark, which includes various scenarios and evaluation protocols, contributing to the advancement of video super-resolution research. The exponential growth in mobile device usage and location data availability poses significant challenges for urban researchers in extracting and managing vast amounts of geospatial data from crowds.  Current methods for collecting geospatial data from crowds through mobile devices suffer from issues like low coordination, high density, and uneven coverage, all while posing privacy concerns for participants.  Existing methods for sampling spatial data, such as methods that rely on user interactions or that utilize their movement patterns, encounter difficulties in balancing equity, efficiency, and privacy. In this research, we propose an efficient and fair sampling method that utilizes the movement patterns of mobile devices to collect geospatial data in an equitable and energy-efficient manner.  This method leverages the fact that the probability of a device visiting different locations in a city follows a Zipf distribution and uses a random walk to generate a set of location weights that reflect the distribution of frequencies of visitation.  It then utilizes these weights to determine the most equitable and efficient subset of locations to visit among all possible subsets.  Experiments conducted using real-world location data from over 13,000 devices demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing methods by a significant margin in terms of equity, while also achieving substantial energy savings of up to 45%.  Furthermore, the method demonstrates excellent scalability and precision in scenarios with varying numbers of devices, locations, and frequency distributions.  The method has been implemented and is currently being utilized to collect geospatial data from crowds through mobile devices at Cornell University.  The method has the potential to be adapted for use in other urban settings with diverse spatial structures and activity patterns. In typical WaveNet, each dilation factor corresponds to a distinct autoregressive probability calculation, thus requiring separate predictions for every factor. However, due to the periodic nature of pitch, our Quasi-Periodic WaveNet aggregates predictions for factors with relatively short ranges, thereby reducing the number of necessary calculations and effectively incorporating pitch-sensitivity into the model. Experiments revealed that this approach not only simplifies the network architecture but also yields superior performance in generative tasks for speech and polyphonic music, surpassing state-of-the-art benchmarks in various metrics. Planetary atmospheres on planets orbiting cooler G-K stars undergo chemical reactions that are primarily powered by stellar light, which generates varying molecular species depending on the system.  As a result, understanding photochemical processes and species formation is crucial for interpreting exoplanet transmission spectra and possible biosignatures.  This study leverages a complex atmospheric model, combining it with a reaction network and species formation tools, to analyze how photochemical reactions, species formation, and system parameters interact on planets orbiting cooler G-K stars.  It focuses specifically on planets similar to Kepler-167 d, located in the habitable zones of three different stars, as well as super-Earths on closer orbits around two suns and Earth-sized planets on orbits around an A-type star.  It explores how various factors affect the composition of their atmospheres, including the strength of the star's light, atmospheric mass, and how many particles are scattered by the atmosphere.  It uses this knowledge to predict the compositon of these exoplanets' atmospheres and provides recommendations for future transmission spectroscopy missions to detect biosignatures in temperate exoplanets.  It prioritizes the Earth-sized planets around the two suns and the 1.5 Earths around Kepler-167, recommending that future transmission spectroscopy missions prioritize the two suns and consider Kepler-167 D if the model is refined further. In higher category theory, the shadow functor is a key construction that creates fractions within categories, resulting in categories of fractions. Our investigation reveals that the shadow functor behaves much like a bicategorical mark, essentially a localizer, which directly influences its underlying properties. We then explore how the category of fractions is derived from the category of marks, establishing a direct relationship between them. This understanding, in turn, allows us to reevaluate the properties of the category of fractions and its associated functor. We also explore localizers in categories of marks and their connection to marks in categories of fractions. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the category of fractions can be viewed as a category of marks, providing a foundation for further study into the properties of localizers in categories of fractions. Acoustic structures are continually being used in various applications with the ongoing development of technology, yet we are seeing a growing need to analyze these structures numerically to better comprehend their behavior.  Both Rayleigh-Schr\"{o}dinger and Schr\"{o}dinger forms of wave equations can be employed to numerically examine acoustic structures, resulting in the generation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors which represent the structural frequencies and corresponding mode shapes.  This study focuses on explicitly defining the structural frequency eigenvalue equation using a Schr\"{o}dinger form and then implicitly defining it using a Rayleigh-Schr\"{o}dinger form; we then develop an inverse approach to determine the structural parameter $p$ in the Schr\"{o}dinger form given the potential $q$ in the Rayleigh-Schr\"{o}dinger form.  An illustrative example is provided to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed method.  The aim of this research is to provide a theoretical basis for developing numerical methods to determine mode shapes and frequencies within acoustic structures.  Such methods can, in turn, contribute to the advancement of innovative acoustic technology by facilitating numerical exploration and optimization of complex structures.  Therefore, we invite mathematicians to engage with this problem by accepting the inverse challenge presented in this study.  The problem is defined as follows: given the Schr\"{o}dinger form of the wave equation with its corresponding eigenvalue equation, determine the structural parameter $p$ in order to derive the Rayleigh-Schr\"{o}dinger form of the wave equation with its eigenvalue equation.  An illustrative example is provided to facilitate understanding of this challenge.  The proposed method provides an explicit solution to this problem.  Theoretical analysis and numerical verification are also provided to validate the method.  The method relies on the explicit solution to the integral form of the integral equation obtained from the boundary layer reduction of the Schr\"{o}dinger form of the wave equation.  The proposed method is applicable to acoustic structures with constant density and the wave equation described by the Helmholtz equation.  The method can be extended to analyze ferromagnetic materials by modifying the potential $q$ to account for the effects of an external magnetic field.  The method can also be adapted for use with the time-dependent Schr\"{o}dinger form of the wave equation.  Theoretical analysis and numerical verification demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method.

This study introduces the concept of quantum immanents for representations associated with Schur algebras, extending a notion from classical immanents. Specifically, we define double Young-Capelli bitableaux and demonstrate their equivalence to products of representations, paralleling the classical Capelli method. From this, we derive altered Schur functions as a combination of these bitableaux, connecting them to plethysm relations. Our findings also link quantum immanents to combinatorial objects, revealing connections through the symmetrizable Cartan matrix and Dynkin diagram, and demonstrating the combinatorial nature of certain Schur algebra results. Finally, we establish relationships between quantum immanents, double Young-Capelli bitableaux and the combinatorial objects known as (p,t)-hook formulas. Our analysis expands upon prior work by J. Shalaby and A. Zeidan in "Quantum Capelli operators and Schur algebra", and our results answer open questions posed there. Additionally, this study provides answers to further questions posed by A. M. Zeidan in a personal communication.
